controls.evidence: We compare our method with several state-of-the-art approaches for VSG

controls.description: Re-run at least one strong offline baseline under the same online constraint (e.g. causal masking so it only sees past segments), giving a like-for-like streaming comparison instead of only online-versus-offline numbers.
controls.evidence: We also implement an online variant of NaSVA [@li2024multi], which introduces causal masking in the transformer encoder's self-attention layers to restrict attention to past segments only.

controls.description: Report a memoryless per-segment baseline: the same off-the-shelf pretrained model applied to each segment independently, with no past context or temporal prior, to isolate the gain attributable to using past segments.
controls.evidence: [BaGLM]{.smallcaps} consistently improves the performance of the underlying LMM it is applied to across all segment durations

controls.description: Evaluate the approach on several different pretrained multimodal backbones (not a single model), to show the conclusions do not hinge on one backbone.
controls.evidence: considering different LMMs: InternVL2.5 8B [@chen2024expanding], InternVL3 8B [@zhu2025internvl3], LLaVA-OneVision 7B [@li2025llavaonevision], and Qwen2.5 7B [@bai2025qwen2]

controls.description: Sweep the duration of the streaming segments (e.g. from 1 to 4 seconds), since too-short segments lack visual cues and too-long ones span several steps.
controls.evidence: Segments that are too short may lack sufficient visual cues to evaluate the video-step alignment or the progress, while longer ones may span over multiple actions, making it harder to localize steps precisely.

controls.description: Measure per-segment processing latency (video decoding plus all model queries, as a function of the number of candidate steps) against the segment duration, to verify that the method really runs in real time on a stream.
controls.evidence: Importantly, the majority of the segments are processed in under 2 seconds, implying that the 2-second segments can be processed in real time.

fruitful_directions.description: Use an off-the-shelf large multimodal model zero-shot as the per-segment step scorer: prompt it with the current segment, the task goal and all candidate steps plus a 'none' option as a single multiple-choice question, and normalise the answer-token probabilities into a distribution over steps.
fruitful_directions.evidence: Surprisingly, models such as InternVL [@chen2024expanding] could already surpass state-of-the-art training-based methods [@li2024multi; @mavroudi2023learning], despite only having access to a single segment at a time.

fruitful_directions.description: Inject past information with a recursive Bayesian filter: keep a running belief over steps, propagate it through a step-transition model (predict) and re-weight it with the zero-shot model's per-segment probabilities used as the observation likelihood (update), with no training and no storage of the full history.
fruitful_directions.evidence: This confirms that the Bayesian filtering formulation is effective
fruitful_directions.section: Ablation studies (oracle step dependencies and progress)

fruitful_directions.description: Build the step-transition model without training from a language model's estimates of which steps are prerequisites of others, and adjust it online with the multimodal model's estimates of step progress (favour steps whose prerequisites are done and whose successors are not).
fruitful_directions.evidence: Thus, accounting for the dependency matrix (and if prerequisites are met) tends to improve performance by reducing the score of non-executable actions.

sterile_directions.description: Making an existing offline, training-based grounding model online by causal masking (restricting it to past segments) and using it as the main approach: its accuracy drops below its offline version and stays well below the training-free zero-shot approach.
sterile_directions.evidence: When evaluated under the same online setting, NaSVA's performance drops to 46.1 R@1 on HT-Step and 24.2 on Ego4D Goal-Step

sterile_directions.description: Scoring each segment with one independent binary yes/no query per candidate step instead of a single multiple-choice query: no consistent accuracy gain (3.4 points worse on one dataset, 0.5 and 1.7 points better on the others) for K queries per segment (about 8.6 times slower in the paper's example), which undermines real-time online use.
sterile_directions.evidence: However, the binary formulation requires querying the LMM $K$ times per video segment, once per candidate step, whereas the multi-choice formulation requires only one query per segment.
sterile_directions.section: Additional analyses (Binary vs multi-choice VSG prompt, Appendix)

taches.questions:
Grounding procedural steps in videos is crucial for enabling machines to follow along and assist humans in complex tasks such as cooking a recipe, assembling furniture, or performing maintenance work. This ability is particularly valuable for real-time procedural guidance in augmented and extended reality applications, where recognizing task progress allows users wearing headsets or smart glasses to receive timely, step-specific instructions. The task of Video Step Grounding (VSG) takes as input a list of procedural steps extracted from an instructional article (e.g., a recipe or a how-to guide) and a video of the same task, and aims to identify which of the steps are performed in the video, that is, which step, if any, each part of the video depicts (a segment may also show an action outside the listed steps).

Existing VSG approaches align procedural step descriptions with their corresponding video frames. Earlier works relied on weakly-supervised learning from instructional narrations, while more recent methods increasingly leverage language models and large-scale pretraining, for instance using language models to turn noisy narrations or speech transcripts into steps and pseudo-labels for training. These strategies face two key limitations. First, they need a training set, entailing the cost of collecting (and potentially annotating) it; moreover, a training set can bias models toward the specific videos and procedural tasks it depicts, limiting their generalization capability. Second, they assume offline processing, where the entire video is available ahead of time, which makes them unsuitable for real-world applications that process a live video stream and must make decisions as it unfolds.

This calls for addressing VSG online and without training: video segments arrive one after the other, and whether the current segment depicts a given step must be decided using only that segment and the segments preceding it, with no task-specific training data. This setting is challenging. Predictions must be made from partial evidence, and without the task-specific representations that would typically be learned from a dedicated training set. The task also requires fine-grained video understanding, since key steps of instructional tasks often involve similar objects or scenes: "inserting a screw" or "aligning parts" may look alike in tasks such as "Assemble a chair" and "Fix a table", making them hard to distinguish without nuanced semantic understanding. Large pretrained multimodal models have demonstrated impressive zero-shot performance on a wide variety of tasks without further tuning, and work on video-language alignment has moved away from frame-caption embedding similarity, which struggles to capture temporal dynamics, toward such models; yet whether off-the-shelf models can ground procedural steps when they only see the current short segment remains an open question. Moreover, a prediction made from the current segment alone has no memory of what has already happened in the video, so uncertain observations cannot benefit from past evidence, while storing and reprocessing the whole history is impractical on a live stream.

The research questions are therefore: can video step grounding be performed online, on a streaming video and without any training, at a level competitive with training-based offline methods? And how can knowledge from past segments be injected into the prediction for the current segment, without storing the whole history and while preserving a zero-shot, training-free approach?

compute.evidence: The paper reports wall-clock time and the size of the cluster, not GPU-hours, so the total is converted. Training: "Our full training pipeline was executed on a cluster equipped with 64 NVIDIA H800 GPUs"; stage 1 ran "approximately 40 hours, spanning a total of 9,000 optimization steps" and stage 2 "around 7 hours of computation and was conducted for 1,500 steps", i.e. 64 x (40 + 7) = 3,008 H800 GPU-hours. Design experiments: "We conducted experiments on a single H800 GPU" with "a continuous 48-hour hallucination run" for each of six targets, for the proposed model and for the baseline pipeline, i.e. about 48 x 6 x 2 = 576 GPU-hours. Benchmark inference (a few hundred complexes at seconds to minutes each) and the consistency-baseline distillation runs are not quantified in the paper and are not included, so about 3,584 H800 GPU-hours is a lower bound on the full budget.

controls.description: The unaccelerated reference model must be run in its full configuration (all recycling cycles and all diffusion sampling steps) on the same benchmarks and scored with the same metrics, as the accuracy target that the accelerated predictor has to match; a proposal is checkable on whether it names this full-iteration upper-bound reference.
controls.evidence: The original configuration of AlphaFold3 employs the full set of recycling cycles and diffusion steps, serving as a strong baseline as well as the reference target

controls.description: A training-free reduced-compute control: the very same pretrained weights evaluated with the reduced budget the accelerated model will use (a single sampling step and a single recycling cycle, with tuned solver settings but no retraining), so that any claimed gain is attributed to the proposed training and not to the cheaper schedule alone.
controls.evidence: AlphaFold3 configured with a single sampling step and a single recycling cycle, serving as a reference baseline without retraining.

controls.description: Existing generic few-step distillation / consistency-training schemes from the generative-modelling literature must be trained and evaluated under the same budget as competing acceleration baselines, not only the slow model and the proposed one; a plan that compares against nothing but the unaccelerated model fails this control.
controls.evidence: We conduct experiments on feasible generic consistency-model baselines, including CD [@song2023consistency], sCM [@lu2024simplifying], ECM [@geng2024consistency]

controls.description: Measured wall-clock inference time on the same hardware, reported next to accuracy and broken down by input size (sequence or token-count bins), rather than a single average speedup factor; the plan must state how runtime is measured and stratified, since the speedup depends strongly on input length.
controls.evidence: we report detailed bin-wise runtime statistics on the Posebusters V2 benchmark
controls.section: Experiment Details / Runtime Characteristics Across Sequence Lengths

controls.description: A leakage control on the evaluation data: evaluation restricted to structures released after the training cutoff (and homology-filtered held-out sets), with the exclusion rule stated explicitly, so that the accelerated model is not scored on complexes seen during distillation.
controls.evidence: All entries predating the training cutoff are excluded from evaluation.

controls.description: Distributional rather than single-sample scoring: draw several samples per input and report the worst-case as well as the best-case accuracy at multiple error thresholds (plus sample diversity and model confidence), so that a method which merely sharpens or collapses the output distribution cannot be mistaken for one that improves accuracy.
controls.evidence: we report the proportions of generated poses whose best and worst RMSDs (with respect to the ground-truth structure) fall below the thresholds of 1, 2, 3, and 5
controls.section: Experiment / Structure Prediction (Metrics); Diversity and Confidence

fruitful_directions.description: Attack both sources of iteration at once: distil the pretrained model so that consistency is enforced not only across diffusion timesteps but also across the repeated refinement cycles of the representation trunk (successive cycles of a single forward pass supervising each other), which removes the recycling bottleneck that dominates once sampling is already single-step.
fruitful_directions.evidence: we introduce **Dual Consistency**, which applies consistency learning to both the diffusion module and the Pairformer.

fruitful_directions.description: Before any retraining, diagnose and repair the sampler itself: few-step failure comes mainly from the stochastic sampling procedure (extra noise injection and enlarged step size amplifying the bias of the ODE prediction), so switching to a deterministic, properly rescaled one-step ODE sampler already yields roughly correct structures and provides the starting point for distillation.
fruitful_directions.evidence: With a proper choice of ODE parameters, the AF3 ODE solver is capable of generating approximately correct protein structures.

fruitful_directions.description: Make the distillation curriculum size-aware: pair each timestep with its reference at a constant distributional (information-geometric) distance rather than a constant Euclidean time interval, folding the data dimensionality of each example into the schedule so that long and short sequences receive equally difficult targets and training stays stable.
fruitful_directions.evidence: Here we incorporate the data dimensionality $D$ into the training schedule to balance the differences in learning difficulty across amino acid sequences of varying lengths.

sterile_directions.description: Relying on training-free acceleration, i.e. better or higher-order ODE solvers and adaptive noise schedules alone, as the main route to single-pass inference: such solvers do not get down to one or two steps and degrade in the extreme few-step regime, so they cannot deliver the order-of-magnitude speedup the problem requires.
sterile_directions.evidence: While high-order solvers improve efficiency, they rarely reduce the number of sampling steps below 10

sterile_directions.description: Simply dialling down the iteration counts by hand (fewer recycling cycles or fewer denoising steps on inputs judged easy) and accepting the accuracy loss, as the plan's main strategy: this trade is already known to degrade predictive performance and leaves the model's iterative, hard-to-differentiate structure untouched.
sterile_directions.evidence: has attempted to mitigate this by manually reducing the number of recycling iterations on simpler structures, thus trading accuracy for efficiency

sterile_directions.description: Taking an off-the-shelf consistency-distillation recipe from image generation and applying it unchanged to variable-length biomolecular inputs (fixed Euclidean timestep pairing, standard weighting and EMA teacher): this collapses training and destroys accuracy, and the heaviest such variants are not even runnable on long inputs because of memory blow-up.
sterile_directions.evidence: a naive implementation of CD leads to training collapse and severely degrades performance

taches.questions:
Proteins realize their biological functions through intricate three-dimensional conformations, and predicting such structures has long been a central challenge in computational biology. AlphaFold2 marked a breakthrough by combining multiple sequence alignments with geometric constraints in an end-to-end framework, achieving near-experimental accuracy. Building on this foundation, AlphaFold3 reformulates the architecture into an all-atom framework and introduces a diffusion-based structure module, thereby enabling the generative modeling of not only proteins but also a wide spectrum of biomolecular complexes. Consequently, this series of models is widely adopted as a family of foundation models for downstream applications such as virtual screening and protein design. However, AlphaFold3's architecture, which relies on iterative Pairformer recycling and multi-step diffusion, requires substantially greater computational overhead than AlphaFold2, restricting its accessibility in downstream workflows.

More specifically, on long sequences the execution time of AlphaFold3 is measured in minutes, which severely limits its usability in downstream tasks that demand high throughput. For instance, small-scale laboratory screening often requires predictions for thousands of candidates, and when extended to large public databases this number grows to an infeasible scale; protein design tasks typically involve comparable computational demand. Previous work has attempted to mitigate this by manually reducing the number of recycling iterations on simpler structures, thus trading accuracy for efficiency. However, such compromises inevitably degrade predictive performance. Moreover, in hallucination-based design approaches, the multistep iterative refinement process hinders feasible gradient backpropagation, ultimately preventing the broader community from adopting AlphaFold3 as a foundation model for diverse applications.

To accelerate the diffusion process, recent advances in generative modeling have explored high-order solvers and consistency models. While high-order solvers improve efficiency, they rarely reduce the number of sampling steps below ten. Consistency models, on the other hand, have achieved remarkable success in image generation and have benefited from refined training schedules. However, transferring them to an AlphaFold3-style architecture raises two difficulties. First, standard consistency schedules assume fixed-dimensional data and pair timesteps at a constant Euclidean interval, which does not accommodate variable protein sequence lengths: on long sequences even a small step can trigger a drastic distribution shift that demands an unrealistic predictive leap, while on short sequences the same interval provides only a weak learning signal, so training dynamics can become unstable or collapse. Second, the iterative diffusion sampler is not the only source of iteration: the architecture also refines its internal pair and single representations through repeated recycling of the Pairformer trunk, whose cost grows with sequence length and which conventional diffusion-acceleration methods do not address at all.

The open problem is therefore whether an AlphaFold3-class all-atom biomolecular structure generator can be compressed into a predictor that runs in essentially a single forward pass -- removing both the multi-step denoising and the recycling overhead -- while retaining the accuracy of the full iterative model on protein, protein-ligand and nucleic-acid complexes. This matters because accuracy alone is not what blocks adoption: throughput and differentiability do. A useful accelerated model must remain reliable in the tail, not merely on average, since high-throughput screening and design pipelines discard most candidates and are harmed more by occasional implausible structures than by small average losses; it must stay cheap enough to be called thousands of times; and it must be light enough that gradients can be propagated through it, so that design methods which optimize sequences against a folding model become feasible with an all-atom model rather than only with earlier, cheaper architectures. Given this problem, how should one design experiments to establish whether such an acceleration is achievable without a loss of predictive fidelity?

compute.evidence: The paper reports no GPU-hours (it only acknowledges IDRIS/GENCI HPC allocations; its runtime table covers test-time inference only). Estimate from the training details it gives: 'All MaskBit ablations are trained with a batch size of $64$ for $50$k iterations.' One training iteration runs the one-step student (forward and backward), the teacher (forward, with classifier-free guidance), the auxiliary model (forward, plus forward and backward for its own update) and the discriminator (frozen teacher backbone forward on real and generated inputs, backward to the inputs), i.e. about 13 forward-pass equivalents of a roughly 0.3B-parameter transformer on 256 tokens, about 2 TFLOPs per sample, 1.3e14 FLOPs per iteration and 6.5e18 FLOPs per 50k-iteration run, i.e. about 20-40 A100-class GPU-hours per run at 50-100 TFLOP/s effective. The paper describes roughly 50 training runs: MaskGit and MaskBit main runs plus a longer MaskBit run; ablations of the gradient estimator, GAN-only vs distillation-only vs combined, GAN mask ranges, GAN loss weights, teacher CFG, soft-embedding temperature and soft embedding inside the distillation loss; MaskGen-L distillation at several CFG values, distillation plus GAN, reward fine-tuning with single rewards and CLIP-weight sweeps, the Gumbel comparison, GAN-only collapse and MaskGen-XL attempts; Meissonic reward fine-tuning at 1024 px, several times costlier per sample. Adding evaluation (50k-sample ImageNet FIDs over temperature sweeps, COCO-30K and MJHQ-30K, GenEval and HPS, Best-of-N and test-time optimization sweeps, 32-step teacher sampling) gives a total on the order of 2,000 GPU-hours (plausible range about 1,000-4,000).

fruitful_directions.description: Replace the discrete token outputs of the one-step generator with a continuous surrogate: the expected token embedding under the generator's per-position output distribution (softmax of the logits times the embedding matrix of the teacher or of the tokenizer decoder), which is deterministic, fully differentiable, lies in the embedding space the teacher backbone and decoder already accept, and has only a small bias when the logits are concentrated.
fruitful_directions.evidence: We define soft embedding as the expected token embedding under the generator's output probability distribution, serving directly as a continuous surrogate for discrete outputs.

fruitful_directions.description: Use the differentiable outputs for adversarial fine-tuning against real data, with a discriminator made of the frozen pre-trained teacher backbone plus lightweight trainable heads and randomly masked input embeddings as augmentation, trained jointly with the distillation loss kept as a regularizer rather than replacing it.
fruitful_directions.evidence: In practice, the best results are obtained by combining both losses: the Di$\mathtt{[M]}{}$O term preserves faithful distillation from the teacher, while the GAN loss increases robustness and improves final sample quality.
fruitful_directions.section: 14.4 GAN loss reduces Di[M]O's sensitivity to hyperparameters (Appendix)

fruitful_directions.description: Fine-tune the one-step generator end-to-end on differentiable rewards computed on images decoded from the continuous surrogate (e.g., CLIP score for prompt alignment plus an aesthetic/preference reward such as ImageReward), keeping the distillation loss as a regularizer, and optionally optimize the generator's input embeddings at test time against rewards (with multi-start Best-of-N), so that the one-step student can exceed its multi-step teacher on prompt-following and aesthetics.
fruitful_directions.evidence: By combining the reward loss with the Di$\mathtt{[M]}{}$O loss we obtain higher GenEval and HPS scores than the teacher when sampling with 32 steps

sterile_directions.description: Using a Gumbel-Softmax straight-through estimator (hard argmax sample in the forward pass, soft relaxation in the backward pass) as the main gradient pathway through the generator's discrete outputs for GAN or reward fine-tuning.
sterile_directions.evidence: In contrast, Gumbel-Softmax straight-through combines significant bias with high variance, making it unstable for reward- or GAN-based fine-tuning.
sterile_directions.section: 12.4 Summary, Theoretical Justification of Soft Embedding (Appendix)

sterile_directions.description: Refining or distilling the one-step generator with an adversarial (GAN) loss alone, dropping the distribution-matching distillation objective.
sterile_directions.evidence: using only the GAN loss (i.e., omitting the Di$\mathtt{[M]}{}$O objective) fails to produce a competitive generator and can even perform worse than the Di$\mathtt{[M]}{}$O baseline

sterile_directions.description: Fine-tuning the one-step generator on differentiable rewards alone, with no distillation or teacher regularization term, as the main refinement strategy for a teacher that is not already aligned with human preferences.
sterile_directions.evidence: We observe that reward-only fine-tuning can induce reward hacking, producing over-saturated images

taches.questions:
Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) generate discrete data by iteratively replacing masked tokens with predicted unmasked ones, learning to reverse an absorbing-state diffusion process that progressively masks the tokens of a sequence. They have recently achieved strong results across diverse domains, including text generation, image synthesis, and multi-modal understanding and generation. For images, a pre-trained tokenizer (e.g., a VQ-VAE) maps an image to a sequence of discrete tokens and its decoder reconstructs the image from those tokens; generation starts from a fully masked sequence and fills it in over many steps, which makes inference time- and compute-intensive. Building on this success, recent work has shown that these multi-step procedures can be distilled into one-step generators, substantially accelerating inference and reducing computational cost while maintaining competitive quality. For instance, Di[M]O distills a multi-step MDM into a one-step generator through on-policy distribution matching: a one-step prediction sampled from the student is corrupted by the forward masking process, and the teacher's and the student's output distributions conditioned on this intermediate state are matched, with the resulting gradient applied directly to the student's logits so that it never has to pass through the non-differentiable sampling operation.

Despite their remarkable performance, current one-step discrete generators face two fundamental limitations. First, they inherit both modeling and alignment errors from the teacher: existing distillation approaches implicitly assume that the teacher fully captures the target distribution, so imperfections in the teacher's generative modeling and the under-alignment of the pre-trained teacher with downstream preferences are both transmitted to the student during data-free distillation. Second, their discrete token outputs block gradient flow. This prevents the application of key refinement techniques that are widely used to improve one-step generators distilled from continuous diffusion models, such as adversarial (GAN) training, differentiable reward fine-tuning, and test-time optimization of the generator's input with respect to a reward. In text-to-image generation, for example, prompt-following and aesthetic quality are the two primary criteria, and the community increasingly relies on learned reward models and human-preference signals to optimize them directly; but because such rewards operate on decoded images, their gradients cannot pass through the tokenizer decoder and the sampled tokens back to a discrete generator. As a result, current distilled MDM generators have limited flexibility to leverage external knowledge, such as real data, or to incorporate user preferences to better align with downstream objectives.

The gradient-blocking problem is common across discrete modeling tasks. Adversarial training on discrete data, for instance, is challenging because the discriminator must compare generated samples with ground truth while the sampling process is non-differentiable. Prior remedies include policy-gradient estimators such as REINFORCE, which are unbiased but whose gradient variance becomes prohibitive when hundreds or thousands of tokens are generated at once, and differentiable relaxations of discrete tokens such as Gumbel-Softmax (often used with a straight-through estimator) and soft-argmax. However, these methods often introduce biased or high-variance gradients and numerical instabilities, and they have not been systematically applied to one-step discrete generators, in particular for fast visual generation. Moreover, the downstream objectives of interest, such as discriminators and reward models, act on continuous inputs such as the images produced by the tokenizer decoder, so a practical solution must let gradients flow through the existing generation pipeline.

This raises two questions. How can the outputs of a one-step generator distilled from an MDM be made amenable to end-to-end gradient-based training, with gradients that are stable, low-variance and faithful to the true discrete objective, while remaining compatible with the existing teacher and tokenizer? And, once such gradients are available, can post-distillation refinements (adversarial training, differentiable reward fine-tuning, and test-time optimization of the generator's input) let a one-step student correct the errors it inherits from its teacher and better align with downstream objectives such as distribution fidelity, prompt adherence and aesthetic quality?

compute.evidence: The paper reports wall-clock training times, not a GPU-hour total. CIFAR-10: trained on a single NVIDIA A100 or H100 GPU, converging after about 100k steps (about 15 hours), so about 15 GPU-hours. CelebA-64: single H100, full training to 400k steps took about 80 hours, so about 80 GPU-hours. LSUN Bedroom-256: 4 H100 GPUs, training to 400k-800k steps took about 4-8 days, so about 384-768 GPU-hours. Teacher training thus totals about 480-860 GPU-hours (about 670 at the midpoint). Not costed in the paper: the distillation runs (multi-stage chains 100->20->4->2->1 reported at six guidance strengths on CIFAR-10, single-stage 100->1 and 4->1 runs whose per-iteration cost grows with the teacher-to-student step ratio, and the CelebA-64 chain), the lightweight-UNet search over 12 Kac hyperparameter settings scored with 2k-sample FID, and the 50k-sample FID evaluations at up to 200 function evaluations per sample. Adding a few hundred GPU-hours for these gives a central estimate of about 1,000 GPU-hours (plausible range about 600-2,000).

fruitful_directions.description: Distill a many-step finite-speed (Kac) flow teacher into few-step students by endpoint matching: over each student segment, integrate the frozen teacher with several substeps and train the student's single Euler step with an MSE loss to land on the teacher's endpoint, relying on the stability of finite-speed flows to reach 1- to 4-step sampling with only a small loss in sample quality.

fruitful_directions.description: Run the distillation as a multi-stage chain with small step ratios (e.g., 100 -> 20 -> 4 -> 2 -> 1 steps), each stage using the previous student as the teacher, rather than one big jump; this shortens each stage and makes per-stage hyperparameter tuning affordable.

fruitful_directions.description: Apply classifier-free guidance directly in velocity space (unconditional velocity plus a constant strength w times the conditional-minus-unconditional velocity gap), which provably keeps the guided velocity square-integrable (finite kinetic energy) and, with a moderate tuned strength, improves conditional sample quality.

taches.questions:
Diffusion models have catalyzed an enormous research wave in generative modeling. Conceptually, they couple a stochastic forward noising process with a reverse-time ordinary or stochastic differential equation whose density evolution is governed by the Fokker–Planck equation, a linear second-order parabolic partial differential equation. Learning consists of estimating time-indexed scores or velocities and integrating them for sampling. A growing body of work also explores probability-flow backbones: deterministic flows trained via flow matching and its optimal-transport variants, rectified flows, and stochastic interpolants that bridge flows and diffusion.

Yet the partial-differential-equation lens on generative modeling need not be limited to Fokker–Planck. Other classical linear second-order equations, elliptic and hyperbolic, offer different structural advantages but remain comparatively underexplored; Poisson flow models, for instance, recast generation through electrostatics-inspired fields. On the hyperbolic side, recent work has replaced the Fokker–Planck equation with the telegrapher equation (the one-dimensional damped wave equation) and its stochastic Kac representation, in which a particle moves at constant speed and reverses direction at the jump times of a Poisson process. A network is fit by regression to a closed-form conditional velocity of this process and integrated backward in time from noise to data, with each image coordinate following an independent one-dimensional Kac process. The resulting probability flows have a finite propagation speed: starting from localized mass, the distribution remains inside a causal cone, the flow is Lipschitz in Wasserstein distance, and velocity norms, hence kinetic energy, stay globally bounded. Diffusion, by contrast, spreads mass instantaneously with effectively infinite propagation speed, which manifests as stiff, rapidly growing reverse-time velocities and as ill-conditioned fields with Lipschitz blow-ups near the end of denoising; indeed, diffusion arises as a limit of the damped wave equation as the damping and the propagation speed tend to infinity. A finite speed cap thus acts like a built-in stability constraint: trajectories cannot accelerate without bound, and late-time integration is less stiff.

So far, however, these finite-speed flows have been developed only for unconditional image generation, and they lack two ingredients that make diffusion-style generators practical. The first is guided conditional generation. Classifier-free guidance, which mixes conditional and unconditional predictions to steer samples toward a condition, is a standard tool for diffusion models, but it is unclear whether guidance can be carried over to finite-speed dynamics without losing the bounded-energy property that distinguishes them from diffusion, whose kinetic energy can diverge near data time. The second is fast sampling. Practical generators are expected to deliver high-quality samples with very few network evaluations, yet it is unknown whether finite-speed flows can be brought down to a handful of sampling steps, or even a single one, without a severe loss of sample quality, and whether their finite-speed, bounded-energy structure can explain, and ideally guarantee, that a coarse few-step sampler stays close to the full sampling trajectory.

This leads to three questions. How can guided conditional generation be built on finite-speed Kac flows while provably keeping the guided velocity field at finite kinetic energy? How can such flows be turned into few-step, ideally one-step, image generators that preserve both sample quality and the numerical stability benefits of finite-speed probability flows? And can the finite-speed structure provide theoretical guarantees that a few-step sampler remains close to the full flow along the entire generation path, not only in its final samples? Answering them would show whether hyperbolic, finite-speed dynamics can be a credible alternative to diffusion for fast image generation.

compute.evidence: The paper reports neither GPU-hours nor hardware. It reports wall-clock seconds for rating the 22 Time-300B subsets: the proposed pipeline takes 4,687 s in total, of which 4,167 s are GPT-4o-mini API calls and only 520 s local meta-training, few-shot tuning and inference; the baselines take 4,785 s (DataOob), 4,938 s (TimeInf), 152 s (KNNShapley) and 210,000 s (DataShapley, marked with an asterisk); per-dataset rating times on the benchmark datasets are at most about 1,930 s. Estimate, counting all local computation as single-GPU time: about 61 h for the Time-300B runtime comparison (almost all of it DataShapley); about 4 h for rating the 11 benchmark datasets with all methods, plus about 3 h of Optuna tuning of the meta-training (323 s per run); about 23 h for roughly 700 trainings of small downstream models (Linear, CNN, PatchTST, iTransformer, TimeMixer, DLinear, Non-stationary Transformer, Informer) on 4,000-point series or classification sets of at most about 1,100 samples, at about 2 minutes each; and about 10 to 15 h for fine-tuning Time-MoE, Time-LLM and MOMENT on rated subsets. Total roughly 100 GPU-hours, an order of magnitude only (plausible range 40 to 150); LLM API usage is excluded.

taches.questions:
Time series data arise ubiquitously across a broad range of domains, including healthcare, finance, industrial manufacturing, weather forecasting and urban computing, and their characteristics can differ vastly from one domain to another. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have unleashed new potential for exploiting these data in time series tasks such as forecasting, imputation and classification. There are roughly two families of approaches: one fine-tunes or prompts off-the-shelf LLMs with time series converted into a suitable format, while the other trains time series foundation models from scratch on vast time series corpora by adapting LLM-inspired architectures and training strategies. In both cases, the quality of the time series data is critical to model performance: low-quality data can negate the benefits of bespoke technical advances and may even degrade performance. In practice, time series datasets are frequently marred by pervasive quality issues, including missing values, corruption induced by sensor failures, and irregular sampling. Consequently, there is a pressing need to assess, accurately and efficiently, the quality of time series data crawled from diverse domains.

General-purpose data attribution methods, such as influence functions and Shapley-value approaches (together with cheaper approximations such as KNN-based or gradient-based Shapley values), estimate the contribution of individual training samples in a model-agnostic way, but they overlook properties specific to time series such as continuity, temporal dependencies and non-stationarity. Existing attempts at time series data quality estimation therefore stress the need for methods tailored to temporal characteristics. For instance, TimeInf adapts the influence function to time series, drawing on earlier work on infinitesimal robustness for autoregressive processes and on influence functionals for time series, and TimeShap extends the Shapley value, a cooperative game-theoretic attribution method, to time series. However, these methods have largely neglected the fact that real-world time series originate from diverse domains with distinct properties and substantial distribution shifts, which limits their effectiveness to a single domain. Furthermore, both influence-function and Shapley-value techniques struggle to strike a balance between estimation fidelity and computational efficiency: influence functions require computationally intensive Hessian and gradient calculations, while Shapley values incur exponential computational costs.

Recently, estimating data quality through LLM judgments has emerged as a promising approach for text, where carefully designed prompts guide LLMs to produce accurate quality assessments. The underlying rationale is that LLMs are proficient in understanding quality criteria for natural language, such as writing style, required expertise, factual accuracy and educational value. Such efforts point to the potential of LLMs for cross-domain and interpretable data quality estimation, but they remain restricted to text and code, and the time series setting is largely unexplored.

It is therefore tempting to ask whether LLMs can be exploited to determine the quality of diverse time series data. Such an approach could leverage the knowledge of time series from many domains that LLMs acquire during large-scale pretraining, thereby circumventing the prohibitive computational cost of calculating influence functions or Shapley values in a domain-by-domain manner. However, it remains under-explored whether LLMs can truly comprehend the key characteristics that underpin the quality of diverse time series data, and how to effectively steer them to distinguish between high- and low-quality time series according to desired quality criteria. The open problem is thus how to rate the quality of time series data drawn from heterogeneous domains in a way that is accurate, computationally efficient and adaptable across domains.

taches.questions:
Directed graphs (digraphs) model systems with asymmetric relationships, capturing essential structures such as flows, dependencies, and hierarchies that arise in many real-world applications. This makes digraphs particularly well-suited for problems in diverse domains including biology, transportation, social dynamics, and, more recently, image and video understanding, where structured and directional representations are critical for interpretation and reasoning. Consequently, generating digraphs is central to tasks such as simulation, data augmentation and novel instance discovery in domains with directional structure.

Graph generative models aim to learn the probability distribution of a set of observed graphs, enabling the generation of new samples that preserve structural and statistical properties. Such models have shown strong potential in diverse applications, including drug discovery, finance, social network modeling, and medicine. However, most generative models focus on undirected graphs, with only limited efforts on directed settings. The vast majority of works on directed graph generation focus solely on directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), with autoencoders, autoregressive methods and, more recently, diffusion combined with an auto-regressive process; these require the input DAGs to be topologically ordered, which can result in higher computational cost. Other approaches are tailored to specific applications and, therefore, to DAGs. A general digraph generation method, following an auto-regressive perspective, has only recently been proposed, and its implementation is not publicly available, limiting its accessibility for study and evaluation.

Two main factors limit progress in this direction. First, at the modeling level, the directed setting is inherently more challenging than its undirected counterpart: edge directionality greatly enlarges the learnable space (for graphs with 4 nodes, there are 218 possible digraphs, compared to only 11 undirected ones) and introduces a substantially larger dependency space, making the underlying distribution harder to learn. In directed graphs, a model must distinguish the different semantics carried by incoming and outgoing edges. The difficulty is further amplified in settings where domain-specific structural constraints must be respected, such as acyclicity in DAGs. Second, beyond these technical challenges, the lack of standardized benchmarks for directed graph generation is a barrier to rigorous evaluation and fair comparison: existing approaches typically rely only on proxy metrics derived from downstream tasks, failing to directly evaluate generative quality, and there are no established benchmarks to evaluate digraph generative quality systematically.

This raises several questions. How can a generative model be made expressive enough to learn distributions over general directed graphs, capturing directional dependencies and respecting structural properties such as acyclicity, without being restricted to DAGs or relying on a prescribed node ordering? Is it sufficient to extend generative architectures designed for undirected graphs to the directed case, or must such models be explicitly sensitive to directional topology? And how can the generative quality of directed graph generators be evaluated directly and systematically, rather than through downstream proxies, so that different approaches can be compared fairly?

taches.questions:
Transporting mass between probability distributions is a ubiquitous problem in machine learning and beyond. Optimal transport (OT) provides a principled approach to such problems by seeking to minimise the total cost of transportation under a chosen cost function, and computational OT, from Sinkhorn's algorithm to more recent neural approaches, has been applied successfully in domains such as biology and extensively within machine learning. More recently, ideas from the flow-based approaches that have revolutionised generative modelling have been leveraged to solve the entropy-regularised dynamic OT problem known as the Schrödinger bridge (SB): finding the most likely evolution of a population between two prescribed distributions, relative to a reference stochastic process. With a Brownian reference process, the static form of this problem is exactly entropy-regularised OT for the quadratic cost. Flow-based SB solvers offer significant scalability advantages, enabling the approximation of OT maps between high-dimensional continuous datasets such as images. Early flow-based solvers were built on the classical Iterative Proportional Fitting (IPF) scheme, which preserves both marginals only at convergence, requires expensive caching of simulated trajectories and tends to 'forget' the reference measure; such methods have since been superseded by solvers based on the Iterative Markovian Fitting (IMF) scheme, which avoids these issues.

Beyond the standard two-marginal problem, multi-marginal OT seeks a joint coupling over several marginals that minimises a total cost. Tree-structured costs are often considered, as they frequently arise in applications while allowing improved scalability by exploiting the tree structure. In the corresponding tree-structured SB problem, stochastic processes run along the edges of a tree and marginals are prescribed only at a subset of the vertices; with Brownian motion along each edge as the reference, it is an entropy-regularised multi-marginal OT problem with a tree-structured quadratic cost. Star-shaped trees, with marginals fixed on the leaves and an unknown centre, are of particular significance because they correspond to an entropy-regularised form of the Wasserstein barycentre problem. The Wasserstein barycentre provides a natural notion of 'average' for probability distributions and is widely studied because of its importance in applications such as Bayesian learning, clustering and representation learning. Computing barycentres is notoriously challenging. Many successful approaches approximate the solution with a finite set of points, but such in-sample methods struggle to scale as dimensionality increases and cannot generate new samples; alternative methods provide continuous approximations through neural parameterisations, but often require multi-level or adversarial optimisation procedures. To date, the only neural ODE/SDE approach to barycentre computation extends the IPF-based diffusion Schrödinger bridge to the tree-structured SB setting, and therefore inherits the drawbacks of IPF; it has been reported to suffer training instability at low entropic regularisation, struggling to match the prescribed marginals at the vertices.

In parallel, one of the most successful approaches to Wasserstein-2 barycentre computation is the iterative fixed-point method, which repeatedly updates a candidate barycentre by solving for the OT map from it to each marginal and pushing it forward through the weighted average of these maps. It performs strongly and has been observed to converge in only a few iterations, but every iteration requires solving a complete OT problem to each marginal, which is expensive because solving even a single OT problem can be challenging.

This raises several questions. Can a scalable, flow-based solver be built for the tree-structured SB problem, and hence for entropic Wasserstein barycentres, that avoids the shortcomings of IPF-based schemes while being guaranteed to converge to the tree-structured SB solution? In the barycentre case, can the fast convergence of fixed-point schemes be retained without paying for a complete OT solve to every marginal at every iteration? And can flow-based barycentre solvers of this kind offer a viable alternative to existing algorithms for continuous Wasserstein-2 barycentre computation?

fruitful_directions.description: Relax strict equivariance while keeping exact functional consistency by composing a strictly equivariant layer with a learned, input-dependent element of the architecture's symmetry group (output = alpha(weights) applied to beta(weights)), so that transformed inputs map to outputs that may differ by some group element and thus stay in the same functional equivalence class.
fruitful_directions.evidence: By introducing $\alpha$, we aim to relax these constraints, thereby improving both the expressivity and performance of metanetworks.

fruitful_directions.description: Parameterize the input-dependent group element through the continuous part of the symmetry group (per-neuron positive rescalings for ReLU MLPs/CNNs, head-wise invertible matrices for attention), predicted from compact weight statistics as a bounded perturbation of the identity whose magnitude is learnable rather than fixed.
fruitful_directions.evidence: However, when $\epsilon$ is learnable, the learned scaling can deviate further from the identity, leading to a broader scaling range that enhances performance.

fruitful_directions.description: Spend a small parameter budget on such a symmetry-respecting relaxation layer rather than on enlarging the strictly equivariant metanetwork: a few percent of extra parameters in the relaxation layer beats a much larger strictly equivariant model across tasks.

sterile_directions.description: Generating the input-dependent invertible matrices (general linear group elements acting on attention weights) through the matrix exponential of a predicted matrix.

sterile_directions.description: Relaxing invariance in metanetworks that output predictions (letting the invariant readout change under symmetry transformations of the input weights); preserving functional identity for invariant outputs requires strict invariance, so any relaxation must stay in the equivariant layers.

sterile_directions.description: Constructing the relaxed map by prescribing an arbitrary group-valued function alpha(g, theta) and solving for a map F with F(g theta) = alpha(g, theta) F(theta): for a general alpha no such F exists (alpha must satisfy cocycle and stabilizer conditions), and this route is impractical for building metanetworks.
sterile_directions.evidence: Although this approach is theoretically motivated, it is not practical for constructing metanetworks.

taches.questions:
Modern problem-solving increasingly relies on neural networks, which encode vast amounts of information in their trainable parameters during learning, with applications ranging from computer vision and natural language processing to the natural sciences. While these parameters capture rich knowledge, accessing and interpreting it remains a challenge.

Metanetworks were introduced to analyze and process other neural networks by treating their weights, gradients and sparsity patterns as structured inputs. Early work focused on evaluating the generalization of trained networks and revealing properties of their behavior, commonly by flattening the parameters or extracting statistics from them before feeding them into multi-layer perceptrons. Metanetworks have since been applied to extracting structure from implicit neural representations, learning optimizers, editing models, evaluating policies and enabling Bayesian inference. Designing them nevertheless remains challenging because of the complexity and high dimensionality of the structures they operate on.

A major difficulty is functional equivalence: many distinct parameter configurations realize the same input-output function. Swapping two hidden units of a multi-layer perceptron leaves its input-output mapping unchanged, provided their outgoing connections are permuted accordingly, and for networks with tanh activations the input-output mapping is known to determine the architecture and the weights up to permutations and sign flips. Such identifiability results have been extended to broader classes of multi-layer perceptrons and to convolutional networks, and recent work has characterized the symmetry groups of multihead attention and mixture-of-experts layers, establishing necessary and sufficient conditions for functional equivalence. The parameter space is thus only a proxy for the underlying function class, and the map from parameters to functions is not injective. A metanetwork that relies solely on raw parameters therefore risks overlooking the symmetries of the architecture it processes, and may produce incompatible outputs for two networks that compute exactly the same function.

Building on the permutation symmetry of hidden neurons, permutation-equivariant metanetworks have been developed that account for neuron reordering within hidden layers, and more recent architectures extend beyond permutations by incorporating additional symmetries such as scaling and sign changes. Equivariance (for metanetworks that output weights) or invariance (for metanetworks that output predictions) with respect to a symmetry group of the processed architecture guarantees that different parameterizations of the same function are treated consistently. However, these approaches enforce strict equivariance at the level of individual weights, which imposes rigid constraints on the layers and often leads to sparse, less expressive models. Yet the true goal is not to preserve the weights themselves but the functions they implement, that is, to respect the functional equivalence classes of the parameters. Strict equivariance is a sufficient way to achieve this, but it is not clear that it is necessary.

Relaxed or approximate equivariance has emerged elsewhere in deep learning to handle imperfect symmetries in real-world data, for instance through relaxed convolution weights, soft constraints added to the training objective or relaxed group convolutions, and its bias-variance trade-offs have been analyzed theoretically. These relaxations were, however, developed for symmetries that only approximately hold, and often treat equivariance as something to be approximated. In weight space, by contrast, the symmetries are exact and are precisely what defines functional equivalence, so it is unclear how weight-level equivariance could be loosened without breaking the guarantee that functionally equivalent inputs are processed consistently.

This raises several questions. Is strict equivariance necessary for metanetworks? What is the right requirement for a map acting on weights to preserve functional identity, so that functionally equivalent inputs always yield functionally equivalent outputs, and can a requirement weaker than strict equivariance meet it? Can metanetwork layers satisfying such a requirement be built in a principled, practical and trainable way for the architectures whose weights metanetworks commonly process, such as feedforward, convolutional and multihead attention networks? And would moving beyond strict equivariance in this way give metanetworks a better trade-off between symmetry preservation and representational expressivity in practice?

fruitful_directions.description: Use the MLLM's own internal representations, already computed in the normal forward pass, as a training-free localization signal: compare the cached value features (KV cache) of the question's target-object text tokens with those of the image tokens (cosine similarity, aggregated over later layers) to build an object relevance map, which needs no query-key attention weights and therefore works with FlashAttention-style kernels.
fruitful_directions.evidence: we propose to localize target objects by leveraging value features of cached tokens of [MLLMs]{acronym-label="MLLM" acronym-form="plural+short"}.

fruitful_directions.description: Replace exhaustive region search with an informed, object-aware search: extract the target object(s) named in the question, propose candidate regions around the peaks of the relevance map, and spend only a few extra MLLM calls re-ranking the top candidates by the model's yes/no existence confidence before answering from the best region, so that cost grows linearly with the number of candidates instead of exponentially with tree depth.
fruitful_directions.evidence: In contrast, `FOCUS` constructs an object-aware relevance map and directly retrieves the most relevant regions, resulting in *linear* scaling with respect to the number of [FPs]{acronym-label="FP" acronym-form="plural+short"}.

fruitful_directions.description: For global-local-view MLLMs, compute the localization map from the visual tokens of the local high-resolution crops rather than from the downsampled global view, obtaining a higher-resolution map that localizes small objects better.
fruitful_directions.evidence: `FOCUS` significantly benefits from the higher-resolution object relevance map generated based on the local crops.

sterile_directions.description: Building the text-to-image localization map from cached key features (cosine similarity between key vectors), even after stripping the rotary position embeddings, instead of value features: it yields lower accuracy and lower recall of the relevant region.
sterile_directions.evidence: However, directly substituting key features for value features in `FOCUS` results in degraded performance.
sterile_directions.section: 4.3 Ablation studies and hyperparameter sensitivity analysis

sterile_directions.evidence: On high-resolution datasets like HRBench, its performance is only on par with the vanilla [MLLM]{acronym-label="MLLM" acronym-form="singular+short"}.

sterile_directions.description: Hierarchical region-tree search that captions every region with the MLLM and merges the regions whose captions mention the target (DC²-style): it is consistently the least accurate cropping approach and computationally heavy because of region-wise captioning.

taches.questions:
Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) exhibit compelling cross-modal perception and reasoning capabilities on image-text data and have become the de facto standard for visual question answering (VQA), the task of answering a question based on the visual content of an image. However, standard MLLM architectures are not well suited to perceiving and reasoning about small visual details in high-resolution images. So-called global-view MLLMs downscale every input image to the base resolution of their vision encoder (for some widely used models only 224×224 or 336×336 pixels), which discards information; as a consequence, they perform poorly on fine-grained VQA, i.e., on questions whose answer depends on small visual details. Unlike common VQA settings, in which the question-relevant objects are typically prominent in the image, fine-grained VQA concerns targets that may occupy only a tiny fraction of a large, high-resolution image.

More recent global-local-view MLLMs process a downsampled global view together with local crops extracted from the original, unresized image. This dual-view strategy reduces information loss, but it multiplies the number of visual tokens, and because self-attention scales quadratically with sequence length, the computational cost grows rapidly. Moreover, despite having access to fine-grained visual details from all local crops, these models struggle to identify the few visual tokens that are relevant to the question amid the large number of local crop tokens, so their effectiveness on fine-grained VQA still remains limited.

An orthogonal line of work is visual cropping: searching the image for the regions that are relevant to the question and passing only those regions to the MLLM. Existing visual cropping techniques, however, suffer from one or more of three limitations. First, some depend on task-specific fine-tuning: SEAL, for instance, pairs the answering model with a separate visual-search MLLM equipped with additional decoders that is fine-tuned to predict object heatmaps and coordinates, and runs a recursive top-down search, a complex multi-module design that is costly to run. Second, several rely on uninformed, exhaustive search: DC² builds a hierarchical tree of image regions and captions each region with the MLLM, while ZoomEye traverses a hierarchical region tree and scores every visited region with three sequential MLLM forward passes using different prompts, a computation that cannot be simplified or shared across regions, so the cost grows quickly with the depth and breadth of the search. Third, ViCrop avoids hierarchical search by directly computing a question-guided heatmap, but its best-performing variants depend on query-key attention weights and answer gradients, which makes them incompatible with efficient attention implementations such as FlashAttention that never explicitly produce attention weights. Simply asking the MLLM where the target is does not solve the problem either: although many MLLMs are fine-tuned to predict bounding boxes, they often fail when prompted directly for the location of small objects, producing hallucinated or imprecise coordinates.

The open problem is therefore how to make an MLLM look at the right part of a high-resolution image. Can the image regions relevant to a fine-grained visual question be localized without task-specific fine-tuning or auxiliary modules, without an uninformed exhaustive search over the image, and in a way that remains compatible with efficient attention implementations? Can such localization benefit both global-view and global-local-view MLLMs, improving their answers to questions about small details while keeping inference cost low, given that MLLM inference is already computationally expensive? And how favorable an accuracy-efficiency trade-off can be reached relative to existing search-based visual cropping methods?

taches.questions:
Geometry reconstruction is a fundamental problem that enables a wide range of applications in fields such as virtual reality and robotics. In recent years, neural reconstruction methods have gained significant attention; a key advantage of these methods is their ability to represent the geometry of a scene continuously, which can help in many downstream tasks. However, vision-based sensors often struggle in adverse weather conditions, or even become completely unusable when objects are obscured by occlusions.

Radio frequency (RF) sensing, specifically wireless millimeter-wave (mmWave) sensing, can see through occlusions, remains robust under challenging visibility conditions and, unlike X-rays, is not dangerous to humans, making it a compelling alternative for 3D reconstruction. This could open up many applications, for example checking whether the items inside a box are the correct items, are damaged, or pose a threat, without ever opening the box. On the other hand, mmWave resolution is extremely low compared to vision: a single radar image provides far less visual context than a camera image, which makes it hard to extract a 3D reconstruction from one radar image alone. Some prior RF systems have performed 3D point cloud reconstruction or human body tracking by leveraging movement or by emulating larger antenna apertures, but the recovered point clouds are still too sparse and noisy to reliably recover detailed geometry; through-wall human sensing relies on human motion to combat specularity, and deep learning on mmWave radar data has mostly targeted self-driving scenarios, where image resolution matters little. Other works have proposed neural implicit representations for RF sensing, aiming to concentrate scene information out of heavy noise through neural optimization, but these systems are designed for large-scale environments such as streets or satellite imagery and are far from achieving millimeter-level precision. When objects are close to the radar, the propagation characteristics of RF signals change dramatically: incoming waves can no longer be approximated as planar, so processing methods designed for large-scale scenes, such as beamforming, introduce a considerable amount of distortion and noise, often exceeding the noise acceptable for gradient descent and leading to unstable optimization. Existing neural RF reconstruction work is thus either limited to far-range scenes or, for individual objects, evaluated only on simulated data, which for wireless signals cannot come close to representing the complexity of real-world measurements. Meanwhile, the multi-view reconstruction and inverse rendering methods of computer vision (multi-view stereo, neural radiance fields, Gaussian splatting, neural implicit surfaces, physically based inverse rendering) are all derived from RGB images and are not easily transferable to mmWave data: even lensless RGB images can be mapped back to a lens-based imaging model without altering the underlying ray physics, whereas for RF signals such a transformation is fundamentally invalid.

The open problem is therefore to overcome the fundamental dilemma between massive RF noise in the input and the reconstruction of complete, high-resolution, millimeter-level 3D surface geometry of near-range objects, including objects hidden behind occlusions. This is not straightforward, because inferring surface geometry from RF signals differs fundamentally from image-based reconstruction in three main ways. First, wireless systems lack a lens-based imaging model: whereas lenses filter and focus the relevant light rays, radar antenna arrays perform lensless imaging and capture all incoming RF signals without directional filtering, which leads to low signal-to-noise ratios because irrelevant signals cannot be excluded. Second, RF signals and visible light propagate differently: visible light is predominantly scattered diffusely by surfaces, whereas RF signals, whose wavelengths are on the order of millimeters, are dominated by specular reflections, so volumetric rendering techniques designed for scattering-based vision sensors are unsuitable for RF imaging. Third, physically modeling lensless RF measurements is computationally expensive: whereas lens-based rendering samples along 1D rays, modeling what each antenna receives requires accounting for contributions from the full 3D space, leading to cubic complexity that makes naive implementations intractable at millimeter resolution.

How can accurate, millimeter-level 3D geometry of near-range objects be reconstructed from noisy real-world RF measurements, in line of sight and through occlusions, despite lensless imaging, specular reflections and the cost of modeling signal contributions from the full 3D space?

compute.evidence: The paper reports no GPU-hours or cost, only hardware: "Training is performed on 4×RTX 3090 GPUs for Qwen3-1.7B-Base and 8×A100 GPUs for Qwen3-8B-Base." (Appendix 7). Estimate from the training details. Large scale (Qwen3-8B-Base, DAPO-Math-17k, 8×A100): 1,056 gradient steps / 16 per iteration = 66 iterations of 512 prompts × 16 rollouts (540,672 rollouts, responses up to 8,192 tokens); assuming about 2,000-2,500 tokens per response, about 45 min per iteration (rollout about half of the step time, as the paper measures) plus about 15 min of validation after each iteration gives about 66 h × 8 GPUs ≈ 500 GPU-h per GRPO or RL-ZVP run. GRPO-DS-g and GRESO-g need 5.29× and 3.99× the rollouts for the same gradient steps (2,859,008 and 2,159,104 rollouts), i.e. ≈1,100 and ≈920 GPU-h (the -r variants are presumably earlier checkpoints of the same runs), so the large-scale main comparison is ≈3,000 GPU-h; the NuminaMath-CoT 20k runs on Qwen3-8B-Base (GRPO and RL-ZVP) add ≈1,000 GPU-h. Small scale (Qwen3-1.7B-Base, MATH, 4×RTX 3090): 672 / 16 = 42 iterations of 512 × 8 rollouts (172,032 rollouts, up to 4,096 tokens), about 25 min per iteration including per-iteration validation ≈ 70 GPU-h per run; GRPO-DS-g (2.45× rollouts) ≈ 100 and GRESO-g (1.58×) ≈ 85 GPU-h, so ≈325 GPU-h for the main comparison; 11 ablation runs (3 component ablations, 3 + 4 alpha values, 1 symmetric variant) ≈ 770 GPU-h. Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct runs (GRPO, two filtering baselines, RL-ZVP; roughly twice the 1.7B cost) ≈ 600 GPU-h. Total ≈ 5,700 GPU-hours (about 4,000 A100-hours and 1,700 RTX 3090-hours), uncertain by roughly a factor of 2.

controls.description: Standard GRPO baseline, in which prompts whose rollouts all receive the same reward get zero advantage, trained on the same data with the same hyperparameters, pipeline and number of rollouts as the proposed method.

controls.description: Prompt-filtering baselines that discard zero-variance prompts, run in the same pipeline: post-rollout dynamic sampling that oversamples until every prompt in the batch has mixed outcomes (DAPO-style), and pre-rollout prediction and skipping of likely zero-variance prompts (GRESO-style).

controls.description: Compute-matched comparison with the filtering baselines: at least one comparison at the same total number of rollouts (sampled responses), with rollout counts reported for every method because filtering spends extra rollouts; a comparison at the same number of gradient steps may be added.
controls.evidence: For GRPO-DS and GRESO, we report results under two settings: *(r)* using the *same number of rollouts* as RL-ZVP for a fair comparison, and *(g)* using the *same number of gradient steps*.

controls.description: Ablation that uses only the all-correct (positive) zero-variance groups, or only the all-incorrect (negative) ones, to measure the contribution of each type of zero-variance prompt.
controls.evidence: Ignoring either negative or positive prompts yields comparable performance, confirming that both play similar roles in providing learning signals for the policy models.

controls.description: Sensitivity sweep of the strength of the signal taken from zero-variance prompts relative to the ordinary group-relative signal, from very small to very large values (ideally across orders of magnitude, zero recovering the standard baseline).
controls.evidence: overly small values fail to sufficiently utilize learning signal from zero-variance prompts, while overly large values may cause unstable training with large gradient updates

controls.description: Experiments in at least two model-scale and training-data regimes of different difficulty, covering both a regime dominated by all-incorrect groups (data hard for the model) and one where all-correct groups become frequent (easier data).
controls.evidence: We conduct experiments on both Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base [@yang2025qwen3technicalreport; @liu2025itrickstrapsdeep] to assess performance across model scales.

fruitful_directions.description: Exploit zero-variance prompts instead of filtering them out: give a non-zero, correctness-signed advantage to groups whose rollouts are all correct (reward) or all incorrect (penalty), while keeping the standard group-relative update for groups with mixed outcomes, so that rollouts already paid for contribute learning signal.
fruitful_directions.evidence: leveraging such prompts brings greater benefits than discarding them, directly challenging the prevailing practice adopted in recent works

fruitful_directions.description: Set the magnitude of the zero-variance advantage token by token according to token entropy (larger updates for high-entropy decision-point tokens in all-correct responses), with a small scaling factor (around 0.1) so that raw entropy values do not produce exploding updates.
fruitful_directions.evidence: The key idea is to scale each token's gradient update in proportion to its entropy.

fruitful_directions.description: Treat all-incorrect groups asymmetrically: lower the probability of every token, but penalize confident (low-entropy) tokens most and high-entropy branching tokens least (e.g. a penalty proportional to the response's maximum token entropy minus the token's entropy), to preserve exploration of alternative reasoning paths.
fruitful_directions.evidence: For incorrect responses, the probabilities of all tokens are reduced, but high-entropy tokens (that initiate reasoning paths and behaviors) are penalized less severely

sterile_directions.description: Exploiting zero-variance prompts with a uniform, sample-level +1/-1 advantage (rewarding all-correct and penalizing all-incorrect responses with the same weight on every token) as the main approach.
sterile_directions.evidence: removing the entropy scaling factor (*e.g.*, using only sample-level +1/-1 as the advantage) causes the most severe degradation

sterile_directions.description: A symmetric token-level scheme in which all-incorrect responses are penalized in proportion to token entropy (the exact negative of the reward used for all-correct responses), so that high-entropy tokens receive the largest penalties.
sterile_directions.evidence: We observe that enforcing symmetry significantly harms performance: the symmetric variant underperforms RL-ZVP across all benchmarks and even falls below the GRPO baseline.
sterile_directions.section: Appendix 9.2 Comparison with a Symmetric Variant of RL-ZVP

sterile_directions.description: Treating zero-variance prompts purely as wasted compute and making better prompt filtering (pre-rollout prediction and skipping, or post-rollout oversampling and discarding) the main strategy, rather than extracting learning signal from them.
sterile_directions.evidence: Under the fair setting with the same rollout budget, RL-ZVP substantially surpasses both GRPO-DS-r and GRESO-r across all benchmarks

taches.questions:
Recent frontier models such as OpenAI o1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, DeepSeek-R1 and Kimi k1.5 provide compelling proof of concept for leveraging long chains of thought to enhance the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). Following these advances, Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) techniques such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and Dynamic Sampling Policy Optimization (DAPO) have emerged as the de facto standard for strengthening LLM reasoning. In RLVR, the policy model is trained by sampling multiple responses (rollouts) to a prompt, checking each final answer against a ground-truth answer, and then reinforcing correct answers while penalizing incorrect ones. GRPO, a variant of Proximal Policy Optimization that dispenses with a costly value model, computes the advantage of each response by normalizing its reward with the mean and standard deviation of the rewards in its group.

This works well when the responses to a prompt contain both right and wrong answers, but it does not account for the case where a group of rollouts is entirely correct or entirely incorrect and therefore receives identical rewards. Such prompts are referred to as zero-variance prompts. For them, the normalized rewards (the advantage values) collapse to zero, so there is no training signal and all rollouts for those prompts are rendered uninformative. Put differently, the policy is rewarded for a correct response only when at least one incorrect response exists in the same group, and penalized for an incorrect response only when at least one correct response is present. Zero-variance prompts typically arise when a problem is too difficult or too easy for the current model: early in training, when the model often fails to solve a problem even once across multiple attempts, and near convergence, when it has become strong enough to solve many problems in every attempt.

Ignoring these prompts may seem conceptually reasonable, but it remains problematic because rollout generation is itself a major bottleneck in RL training, so the compute spent sampling responses to zero-variance prompts is simply wasted. Recent methods acknowledge this inefficiency and try to filter zero-variance prompts out, either before rollout, by predicting from the training history which prompts are likely to yield identical rewards and skipping them, or after rollout, by repeatedly sampling and discarding them until a batch contains only prompts with mixed outcomes. These methods view zero-variance prompts merely as a cost to be avoided and implicitly assume that they offer no value for policy optimization. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has investigated whether zero-variance prompts themselves can serve as a valuable source of learning signal.

This raises several open questions. Can the responses to a prompt whose rollouts are all correct, or all incorrect, provide meaningful feedback for policy optimization, even though the group contains no contrasting response? If so, how should such feedback be formulated so that it remains informative and does not destabilize training? And would exploiting these prompts, instead of discarding them, lead to better reasoning performance and more stable learning than both standard group-relative training and the prevailing practice of filtering them out?
