taches.questions:
Recording dynamic scenes from multiple viewpoints has become increasingly common in everyday life. From concerts and sports events to lectures and birthday parties, people often capture the same moment using different handheld devices. These multi-view recordings present a rich opportunity to reconstruct scenes in 4D, enable bullet-time effects, or enhance the capabilities of existing vision models. However, these videos are typically captured independently, without synchronization or known camera poses, making it difficult to align and fuse them coherently.

The task is the following: given a set of asynchronous videos that capture the same dynamic scene from different viewpoints, estimate a time offset for each video, to be applied to its original out-of-sync clock, so that after correction frames sharing the same clock time correspond to the exact same moment across all videos.

Existing synchronization methods rely on controlled environments, manual annotations, specific patterns such as human pose, audio signals such as flashes or claps, or expensive hardware setups such as time-coded devices, none of which are available in casually captured videos. Human-centric approaches, which use body pose as the synchronization signal, are limited by the accuracy of pose estimation and by the number of people present, and they struggle in scenes without prominent human activity. Audio-based approaches only work in quiet environments and do not carry over to in-the-wild settings where audio is noisy or unavailable. Methods that jointly optimize camera poses and temporal offsets within a learned scene representation are often constrained to specific environments or object types. Geometry-based methods estimate temporal offsets from multi-view geometric constraints, but typically assume static scenes or a fixed viewpoint. Meanwhile, structure-from-motion and learned camera-pose estimators recover camera geometry accurately, yet they rely predominantly on static visual cues and therefore fall short of synchronizing dynamic scenes.

Building a practical and robust synchronization system that works on videos in the wild is challenging. Camera poses are unknown and cameras may move, so the geometric relationship between each pair of cameras must itself be estimated reliably. The moving objects that carry the timing information are not known in advance and are generally small and blurry. Associating points across cameras with significantly different viewpoints is difficult. The offsets to be recovered are continuous, while observations arrive only at discrete frame times. Finally, not all views overlap, so some pairs of cameras may share little spatial or temporal overlap.

This raises several questions. How can a set of casually captured, unposed and unsynchronized videos of the same dynamic scene be aligned in time with high precision, without specialized capture, audio, manual correction, or assumptions about the scene content such as the presence of people? Which visual evidence can reliably reveal the temporal offset between two cameras whose poses are unknown and possibly changing over time? And how can a single, globally consistent offset be recovered for every video when the evidence relating some pairs of views is weak, ambiguous or missing? Answering these questions would open the door to scalable, unconstrained multi-view 4D scene understanding and to downstream tasks, such as 4D reconstruction of dynamic scenes, that depend on synchronized input.

It reports only the hardware and the training schedule: in the appendix on computational resources, We train all models on 2 H100-80GB GPUs, and in the hyperparameters appendix, 100 epochs with a batch size of 128 and a global batch size of 512. Estimate: the main training set has 622,766 building-block graphs with one conformer drawn per molecule per epoch, so a global batch of 512 gives roughly 1,200 optimizer steps per epoch and about 1.2e5 steps for a 100-epoch run. The backbone is a small SE(3)-equivariant network over at most 5 building blocks (a few tens of atom slots), so a step costs on the order of 0.2-0.4 s on 2 H100s, i.e. roughly 10 h wall clock, about 20 GPU-hours per 100-epoch run. The paper describes several such runs: the main model (100 epochs), the pharmacophore-conditioned model, a motif-scaffolding fine-tune, a model on the larger vocabulary dataset (50 epochs), six training ablations at 50 epochs, and SemlaFlow retrained on the same data for 150 epochs, plus sampling of 1000 molecules per configuration for many sampling ablations. Summing these gives roughly 150-250 GPU-hours, hence an order-of-magnitude figure of about 200 GPU-hours. Excluded, because they are CPU work: dataset conformer generation (ETKDG, MMFF94 and GFN2-xTB over millions of conformers), single-point energy evaluation, retrosynthesis search and docking, which together likely dominate the total compute cost in CPU-hours.

taches.questions:
Generative models significantly enhance the efficiency of chemical space exploration in drug discovery by directly sampling molecules with desired properties. However, a key bottleneck in their practical deployment is low synthetic accessibility: generated molecules are often difficult or impossible to produce in the laboratory. To address this limitation, recent work has turned to template-based methods that emulate the chemical synthesis process by constructing synthesis trees that link molecular building blocks through known reaction templates. These representations, while useful for downstream experimental validation, do not describe the underlying 3D geometry and thus cannot capitalize on the conformational information that is often crucial for diverse chemical and biological properties.

Parallel advances in generative molecular design have explored spatial modeling at the atomic level. Inspired by advances in protein structure prediction and by generative frameworks such as diffusion and flow matching, recent work has focused on directly sampling 3D atomic coordinates of small molecules, learning to generate spatially meaningful, property-aligned conformations along with molecular graphs. The ability to model atomic coordinates directly increases the expressivity of these approaches, enabling applications such as pocket-conditioned generation, scaffold hopping, analog discovery, and molecular optimization. However, without considering practical synthesis routes, integrating synthesizability constraints into these models remains a major challenge, and most existing 3D generative approaches do not ensure that proposed molecules can be made in practice. While recent work has addressed synthesizability for 2D molecular graphs, extending such constraints to 3D, and to geometry-based conditional generation, remains largely unexplored.

Several obstacles stand in the way. Directly optimizing synthesizability scores is often unreliable, so the predominant route to synthetic accessibility has been to assemble molecules from commercially available building blocks joined by known reaction templates; yet such generators typically emit only molecular graphs and no atomic coordinates. The representations commonly available for 3D work are also ill-suited to synthesis awareness: synthon-based representations do not guarantee that a valid synthesis route exists, do not provide one even when it does, and lack the flexibility to constrain the reaction space, which matters when one wants to prioritize high-yield, high-reliability reactions or to remain within the limits of automated synthesis platforms. Relying instead on external, black-box reaction simulators to couple building blocks offers no fine-grained control when a reagent has several reaction centers, and such steps do not define atom mappings between reactants and products, making it impossible to trace product atoms back to their parent building blocks. A further difficulty is that most 3D molecule generation methods require the number of atoms to be specified in advance, which is awkward when the identity of the constituent building blocks is itself still being decided. Finally, the few approaches that do couple synthesis pathways with 3D structure optimize an external reward and typically require a full training run for each target pocket, which is costly and exposes the generator to reward hacking.

This raises the central questions. Can a single generative model sample small molecules so that each sample comes with both a physically realistic 3D conformation and an explicit, traceable route by which it could actually be made, instead of treating geometry and synthesizability as separate concerns handled in sequence or by post hoc filtering? What kind of data and molecular representation would such a model require, given that existing conformer datasets carry no synthesis information and existing synthesis-aware representations carry no geometry? How should synthesizability and geometric quality be measured so that claims of practical makeability are credible rather than an artifact of the scoring tool used? And can one amortized model, once trained, serve the geometry-conditioned design problems that drug discovery actually poses, such as completing or connecting parts of a known three-dimensional ligand, or designing novel molecules that reproduce a desired spatial arrangement of interaction features for a target, without external scoring functions and without retraining for each new target?

taches.questions:
Large language models can be knowledge edited, that is, updated to incorporate new or corrected facts without retraining from scratch. This capability is crucial for keeping models up to date with evolving information and for correcting errors on the fly. Large vision-language models (LVLMs), which combine textual and visual understanding, make knowledge editing even more challenging: they encode factual knowledge in both their textual and their visual pathways, and they require mechanisms that update the knowledge of both modalities consistently. Efficiently editing LVLMs is crucial for real-world applications, such as swiftly correcting critical visual recognition errors (e.g., a model misidentifying Donald Trump as Boris Johnson). However, research on multimodal knowledge editing remains scarce compared with the extensive studies on text-only language models.

Existing benchmarks for LVLM knowledge editing are limited in scope. They typically focus only on visual knowledge updates, such as changing the identity that an image is recognized as, and overlook scenarios in which textual facts about an entity (e.g., its attributes, roles or affiliations) must also be updated. Furthermore, they do not evaluate continual editing, in which multiple knowledge updates are performed sequentially, nor do they test a model's ability to reason compositionally over edited facts. This is a critical gap, because real-world knowledge updates often arrive incrementally and involve intertwined visual and textual information: once a model has been corrected about who appears in a photo and, separately, updated with a new fact about that person, a question about the person in the photo can only be answered correctly by combining both edits.

Existing editing approaches face fundamental difficulties in this setting. External-memory editors store edited knowledge outside the model and retrieve relevant information at inference time without modifying model parameters, which makes them suitable for long-term retention. However, they typically transplant text-based retrieval strategies from language models directly, ignoring visual cues that are necessary for matching multimodal queries to the right edits, which can reduce retrieval accuracy. They also face an internalization issue: the model may over-rely on its stale internal knowledge, especially when the retrieved information conflicts with what it has learned, leading to incorrect answers. Conversely, internal-memory editors embed edits directly into model parameters via fine-tuning or low-rank adaptation, viewing the feed-forward network as a key-value memory that stores in-model knowledge. Although beneficial for internalizing edits, these methods typically store visual and textual edits within a unified representation space, risking cross-modal interference and representation collapse; moreover, sequential internal edits suffer from catastrophic forgetting, degrading previously stored knowledge with successive updates.

This raises several questions. How can an LVLM accommodate a continual sequence of interleaved visual and textual edits so that each new edit takes effect while earlier edits are retained, without interference between modalities? How can separately edited visual and textual facts be integrated to answer compositional queries that require both, even when externally retrieved evidence and the model's internal knowledge disagree? And how can editors be evaluated in this continual and compositional setting, which existing benchmarks do not cover?

compute.evidence: Not reported in GPU-hours; the paper states that all experiments were run on 2 NVIDIA A6000 GPUs with mixed precision. Main generative training: the configuration table gives 100 epochs at batch size 12 over 37,003 training sequences (about 3.7 million sequence samples), and the loss curves show about 50k steps for stage 1, 50k-70k for stage 2 and a cosine-decay stage 3 beyond 70k, i.e. roughly 100k-150k steps in total. With a frozen Stable-Diffusion-2.1-sized U-Net, a trainable control module over 3 input frames and a frozen DeepSeek-VL2 providing semantic features, assuming about 2 s per step on the two A6000s gives about 55-85 h of wall-clock time, i.e. about 110-170 GPU-hours (about 150 retained). Adding the training of the MLLM temporal adapters and the automatic captioning of the 37,003 sequences with Qwen2.5-VL (about 100 GPU-hours), the ablation variants (without time-interval encoding, without the prompt, without semantic fusion, without text guidance, base control block, two prompt variants; about 100 GPU-hours) and the training or fine-tuning of the baselines on the same data (Qwen2.5-VL-7B, DeepSeek-VL2, RSICC-Former, SITSCC, TEOChat, GeoSynth-Canny, MCVD, DiffusionSat; about 150 GPU-hours) gives roughly 500 A6000 GPU-hours, uncertain by about a factor of 2.

controls.description: General-purpose (video-capable) MLLMs fine-tuned on the same training data as the proposed model, including the same backbone without any added temporal mechanism, so that gains from temporal modelling are separated from gains due to the backbone and to fine-tuning.

controls.description: Forecasting baselines covering the main conditioning strategies: a generator guided only by the structure of the last observed image (e.g., its edge map), a video-prediction conditional diffusion model conditioned on past frames, and a metadata-conditioned generative foundation model for satellite imagery.
controls.evidence: our baselines represent three distinct conditioning strategies: (1) Methods relying on single-frame structural guidance, represented by GeoSynth-Canny [@sastryGeoSynthContextuallyAwareHighResolution2024], which uses edge maps from only the last observed image. (2) Approaches adapted from video prediction, represented by MCVD [@voleti2022mcvd], a conditional diffusion model. (3) Models using metadata conditioning, represented by DiffusionSat [@khannaDiffusionSatGenerativeFoundation2024], a generative foundation model for satellite imagery.

controls.description: An ablation in which the forecaster receives no signal from the change-understanding component (conditioned only on the historical images), compared with the understanding-guided forecaster, to test whether understanding of past change actually improves forecast quality and temporal consistency.
controls.evidence: The 'Base Control Block' variant, which lacks both forms of semantic guidance, performs the worst

controls.description: Evaluation on an independent, held-out test set of long-term (multi-year) sequences whose reference change descriptions are written by human experts, rather than produced by the automatic captioner used to label the training data.
controls.evidence: For rigorous and unbiased evaluation, we curated an independent testset of 150 challenging, long-term (5-10 years) sequences from Google Earth. The ground-truth change descriptions for testset were annotated by human experts

controls.description: A check that gains on automatic text metrics are not artifacts of output length, e.g., comparing the average length of generated descriptions with that of the human references for every compared model.
controls.evidence: To address potential concerns about the sensitivity of automatic evaluation metrics (e.g., BLEU, CIDEr-D) to the length of generated text, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of the average word count for all generated descriptions compared to the human-annotated ground truth references on our test set.

fruitful_directions.description: Couple understanding and forecasting by injecting the change-understanding model's internal semantic features (not only its generated text) directly into the diffusion forecaster's control path, as dense multi-scale control signals adaptively fused with low-level structural control derived from the historical images.
fruitful_directions.evidence: injecting the MLLM's deep semantic reasoning directly into the generative control path is paramount for ensuring long-term temporal consistency

fruitful_directions.description: Adapt a frozen MLLM to sparse, irregular, multi-year satellite sequences in a parameter-efficient way, by inserting learnable tokens that encode the actual time interval between consecutive images and by focusing it with a structured change-description prompt, rather than relying on its native video reasoning or on full fine-tuning.
fruitful_directions.evidence: For the temporal understanding task, removing PTE and CTP modules leads to significant performance degradation, most notably dropping TCS score by 23% and 15% respectively.

fruitful_directions.description: Measure the temporal consistency of a forecast by comparing the change between the last observed image and the forecast with the most recent historical change (e.g., location of change centroids and changed area from binary change masks), in addition to pixel and perceptual metrics that cannot penalize temporally implausible futures.
fruitful_directions.evidence: This metric quantifies the temporal plausibility of a forecast by comparing the spatio-temporal dynamics of predicted changes against those of the recent past.

sterile_directions.description: Using a single native unified multimodal model that both understands and generates images (Chameleon- or Janus-Pro-style) as the main model for both tasks; preliminary experiments showed significant performance gaps compared with specialized models.
sterile_directions.evidence: We initially considered native unified models (Chameleon [@team2024chameleon], Janus-Pro [@chen2025janus]) which could theoretically leverage cross-task information more effectively, but preliminary experiments showed significant performance gaps compared to specialized models, making them unsuitable for demanding remote sensing tasks.

sterile_directions.description: Guiding the diffusion forecaster only through text, i.e., generating a change description and using it as a global text prompt or text condition, without injecting richer semantic features into the generator's control; this variant loses a large part of the temporal consistency.
sterile_directions.evidence: Disabling semantic feature fusion ('w/o Semantic Fusion') causes a substantial 18% drop in TCS (from 0.9690 to 0.7911), more severe impact than removing only high-level text guidance.

taches.questions:
Understanding how a scene has changed and forecasting how it will look next from Satellite Image Time Series (SITS) is fundamental to many critical applications, yet it poses a profound challenge: predicting the future requires a deep understanding of past change. Two tasks are central. In temporal change description, given a sequence of temporally ordered satellite images of the same area, the goal is to generate a natural-language description that accurately summarizes the key dynamic changes that occurred over the observation period, such as urban expansion or agricultural cycles; this requires comprehending the temporal evolution and, ideally, the underlying causal narrative of the changes. In future satellite image forecasting, given the same historical sequence, the goal is to generate a plausible image for the next time point. A critical and often overlooked requirement is that the forecast be temporally consistent: the generated changes should be a logical continuation of the trends and dynamics observed in the historical data, not merely a plausible standalone picture.

Although foundation models such as Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) and diffusion-based image generators have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, their application to this domain remains fragmented and fundamentally limited. On the understanding side, static image captioning ignores temporal context, while existing temporal change description methods lack the semantic depth of MLLMs: they fuse information across images through simple interactions, their long-range temporal reasoning is limited, and they struggle to capture why changes occur. General-purpose MLLMs, even video-capable ones, are not optimized for this setting either: video-centric models are typically tuned for densely sampled frames with fixed, short intervals, whereas consecutive satellite acquisitions are sparse and irregular, with gaps that can span several years. On the generation side, single-image synthesis cannot model evolution, and temporal forecasting approaches struggle with long-term consistency because they do not grasp the semantic drivers of change: their conditioning is typically low-level (e.g., edge maps), based on simple metadata, or limited to text guidance, and it lacks fine-grained temporal semantic interaction, so they can generate what a scene looks like but cannot reason about why it should look that way given its history. As a result, change understanding and future forecasting have been treated as disjointed tasks, even though both are limited by a common bottleneck: modeling long-range temporal dynamics.

This raises several questions. How can a model reason about why changes occurred across a long, irregularly sampled sequence of satellite images, and describe them accurately? How can such an understanding of past change be used to generate what will happen next, so that the forecast is a temporally consistent continuation of the observed trajectory rather than only a realistic-looking image? Can enhancing long-range temporal understanding improve performance on both tasks simultaneously, with the understanding of past change directly informing the forecast? Finally, how can the temporal consistency of a forecast be rigorously evaluated, given that standard image-quality metrics cannot penalize a prediction that is perceptually realistic but inconsistent with historical trends?

compute.evidence: No total is reported. The paper states "Pretraining takes approximately 3 hours on a machine with 4 $\times$ NVidia H100 GPUs." (50,000 steps per run, all datasets), i.e. about 12 GPU-hours per pretraining run, and that the POYO+ baseline "required an average of 7.5 hours on 4 NVidia B200s" (about 30 GPU-hours per run), trained across five random seeds (about 150 GPU-hours). Estimated pretraining runs: 4 datasets x 2 pretraining sets (all populations for the transductive settings, test populations held out for the inductive zero-shot setting) = 8; data-scaling sweeps on Allen VC and IBL (about 4 pretraining sizes each) = about 8; ablations (no spatial layers, no neuron dropout, temporal-only layers replaced, spike-based encoder) on about 2 datasets = about 8; bin-size sweep = about 8; about 32 runs x 12 = about 380 GPU-hours. Adding POYO+ (about 150) and the smaller NeuPRINT, NEMO and LOLCAT baselines plus linear probes (about 50) gives about 600 GPU-hours. Unreported hyperparameter line searches or repeated seeds could raise this toward about 1,000.

controls.description: Compares against existing neuron-identity methods of both kinds, run on the same splits: single-neuron feature models (e.g., waveform/autocorrelogram-based or interspike-interval-based classifiers) and population-context models that summarize neighboring neurons with fixed summary statistics.
controls.evidence: We compare `NuCLR` to several baselines: **NeuPRINT** [@neuprint], a population-context model that uses summary statistics of neighboring neurons and the recorded behavior; **NEMO** [@yu2025in], a CLIP-style contrastive approach that encodes individual neurons using their activity autocorrelograms and waveform templates; and **LOLCAT** [@schneider2023transcriptomic], a supervised model that uses the interspike interval distribution for individual neurons and leverages trial structure in the recording.

controls.description: Includes an ablation that removes access to the other neurons' activity (a single-neuron-only version of the same encoder) while matching depth and parameter count, to test whether population context adds identity information beyond a neuron's own activity.
controls.evidence: When ablating the spatial attention layers, the spatial layers were replaced with additional temporal layers to match the overall model depth and parameter count.

controls.description: Tests generalization in a strict held-out (inductive zero-shot) setting: the test sessions/animals are excluded from representation learning, and the frozen encoder and decoder are applied to them without any fine-tuning or retraining.
controls.evidence: (3) *Inductive zero-shot*, where the test populations are entirely unseen during pretraining, and no fine-tuning is performed on the encoder or classifier before evaluation.

controls.description: Splits the decoder's training and test data at the subject or recording level (e.g., leave-one-subject-out), not neuron-wise, so that a classifier cannot succeed merely by recognizing the session or animal when labels are confounded with recordings.
controls.evidence: We did not test classifier performance on this dataset in the transductive setting as a "perfect" classifier only has to infer which of the previously seen sessions does the neuron belong to, and the cell-type corresponding to that session.

controls.description: Checks whether the learned neuron representations are confounded by recording-specific nuisance factors (subject, session or probe identity), e.g., by visualizing the embeddings or decoding these factors from them.
controls.evidence: The subject- and session-specific clustering observed in smaller datasets (Bugeon et al. and Steinmetz et al.) may hinder data-driven discovery, as it suggests entanglement with recording-specific factors.

controls.description: Scores cell-type and brain-region decoding with a class-imbalance-robust metric (e.g., macro F1-score) rather than plain accuracy.
controls.evidence: Our main metric is the **macro F1-score**, which is robust to class imbalance and enables fair comparison across datasets with varying label distributions

fruitful_directions.description: Build each neuron's representation from its own activity together with rich, fine-grained context from all simultaneously recorded neurons (e.g., attention across the whole population that handles populations of any size without a fixed neuron ordering), rather than from single-neuron features or fixed population summaries.
fruitful_directions.evidence: These results highlight the importance of spatial context: integrating information from surrounding neurons provides complementary signals to single-neuron activity and improves the model's ability to capture features of neuronal identity.

fruitful_directions.description: Learn the representations without labels by exploiting the temporal stability of identity: a contrastive objective in which the same neuron observed in two different time windows forms a positive pair and the other neurons of the same population serve as negatives; then freeze the encoder and read out cell type and brain region with linear probes, including zero-shot on new animals.
fruitful_directions.evidence: Because identity-related properties such as cell type or brain region remain static, we encode this temporal-invariance using a contrastive loss that encourages corresponding neurons across the two views to produce similar representations.

fruitful_directions.description: Scale unlabeled pretraining across many animals and measure zero-shot decoding as a function of both the amount of pretraining data and the number of labeled neurons, since adding unlabeled recordings can help more than adding labels.
fruitful_directions.evidence: doubling the amount of pretraining data is significantly more beneficial than doubling the number of labeled neurons

sterile_directions.description: Representing each neuron from its own activity or intrinsic features alone (e.g., its spike-train statistics, waveform, interspike-interval or autocorrelogram profile), without access to the surrounding population's activity.
sterile_directions.evidence: Ablating the spatial layers (population context) led to large performance drops on both the Allen VC (from 0.72 to 0.55) and IBL datasets (from 0.53 to 0.36).

sterile_directions.description: Feeding the encoder per-spike tokens (spike timestamps read by perceiver-style cross-attention) instead of binned, temporally patched activity as the main input representation.
sterile_directions.evidence: We find that this spike-based encoder performs significantly worse on the Allen VC cell-type classification task, while achieving nearly comparable performance on the IBL brain-region classification task
sterile_directions.section: Appendix 6.2 Experiments with a spike-based encoder

sterile_directions.description: Pooling neurons from different probe insertions into one population that interacts inside the model, instead of treating each insertion as its own population; the model then groups neurons by probe rather than by biological properties.
sterile_directions.evidence: In early experiments, we observed that allowing interactions across insertions led the model to cluster neurons based on probe identity rather than biologically meaningful properties.

taches.questions:
Neurons operate in ways that reflect their cell type, connectivity, and the brain region in which they are embedded. Understanding how these structural and physiological factors shape neural activity is an important open question and is central to modern theories of neural function. Cell type- and circuit-specific effects are also increasingly implicated in neurological disorders: particular neuronal subtypes can be selectively affected in neurodegenerative disease, and neuron subtypes can be targeted to improve efficacy in real time in closed-loop brain stimulation. Together, these directions highlight a broader need to understand how features such as cell type and brain region contribute to a neuron's role in the brain, motivating the development of methods that can extract aspects of neuron identity.

Much of what is known about neuronal cell types and their connectivity comes from molecular, anatomical, and morphological labeling techniques that tag neurons based on gene expression profiles or structural features. These approaches have revealed a rich taxonomy of neuronal classes, but they are resource intensive and typically provide only a sparse labeling of one or a few classes at a time, so identity labels are costly and difficult to obtain at scale. There is currently no molecular access to different cell types or projection classes in nonhuman primates and humans, which has created major roadblocks in studying neuron diversity in humans. For these reasons, there is growing interest in methods that can infer aspects of neuronal identity directly from large-scale neural population activity.

Deep learning approaches to this question have only recently begun to be explored. Early methods relied on intrinsic single-neuron features such as waveform shape or interspike interval profiles, but these signals capture only part of what distinguishes one neuron from another. More recent approaches incorporate some information about the ongoing population activity, but reduce the surrounding activity to fixed low-dimensional summaries, which obscures the fine-grained coordination patterns that are often key to neuronal identity. Furthermore, these models usually require retraining or finetuning on each new set of neurons, limiting their ability to generalize in a zero-shot manner across animals.

Making use of population context is itself challenging. The number of recorded neurons varies widely across experiments, individuals, and sessions, making it non-trivial to define a consistent input structure or population-level operation, and recordings span multiple experimental conditions, including different stimuli and behaviors, which makes it hard for a model to generalize across recording sessions. These limitations point to the need for methods that leverage rich population context while producing neuron-level representations that transfer robustly across recordings.

This raises several questions. Can a representation of each individual neuron be learned from population activity, when identity labels are scarce, such that it captures aspects of the neuron's identity such as its cell type and brain region? Can such representations transfer to entirely new sessions and animals without retraining or additional metadata? And how does the identity information they capture depend on the amount and diversity of recordings available for learning, compared with the number of labeled neurons?

compute.evidence: Converted from reported wall-clock time. The paper states 'Training runs on an instance with 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs and takes about 2 days' (Method - Network Training and Inference), and the appendix (Training and Inference Details) splits it into stage 1 (about 1.5 days, 15 epochs on 8,386 samples) and stage 2 fine-tuning (about 1 day, 20 epochs on 2,929 samples): 8 GPUs x 2.5 days x 24 h = 480 A100 GPU-hours (384 with the main text's 'about 2 days'). This covers one full training of the final 5.4M-parameter model; the GPU time of the ablation retrainings, of fine-tuning the 2D face animation and optical flow models, and of generating 2D supervision for thousands of unrigged heads is not reported, so the true total is likely higher.

controls.description: Compare against the existing template-free neural rigging method (NFR) as the main prior-art baseline, run fairly: its inputs get the preprocessing it requires (keeping only the largest connected component, trimming inner lip and eyelid surfaces) and the comparison is restricted to the humanoid heads it was designed for.
controls.evidence: To ensure a fair comparison with NFR [@NFR], each input mesh was preprocessed following the same procedure as in their original implementation

controls.description: Compare against a classical template-based deformation-transfer baseline, which transfers the FACS expressions of an exemplar rigged head to the target mesh using point correspondences (e.g. annotated landmarks), representing the template-based family of auto-rigging methods.
controls.evidence: Another method that we compare to is the Deformation Transfer [@sumner2004deformation], which requires an exemplar expression mesh and user-annotated point correspondences as additional input.

controls.description: Hold out artist-rigged heads (excluded from training and from any data augmentation) as a test set with 3D ground truth, and report per-vertex error against the ground-truth blendshapes on scale-normalized meshes, giving both the mean error and a tail statistic (e.g. 95th-percentile vertex error), computed over all FACS poses of the rig.
controls.evidence: we compute the Mean Absolute vertex Error (MAE) and the 95th-percentile vertex error (MAE Q95) to capture challenging cases; both metrics are evaluated over the full set of 96 FACS poses.

controls.description: Test generalization on out-of-distribution meshes not seen in training: held-out heads of other species and shapes (including non-humanoid ones) and in-the-wild assets from external sources with different topologies, at least qualitatively where no ground-truth rig exists, side by side with the baseline.
controls.evidence: another with unrigged heads featuring diverse species and shapes to assess generalization on out-of-distribution samples, simulating real-world applications.

controls.description: Include a baseline trained only on the scarce rigged meshes with 3D supervision (same architecture, no additional unrigged data or extra supervision), to show that the strategy used to go beyond the rigged set actually improves accuracy and generalization.
controls.evidence: Relying solely on rigged heads for training limits the model's generalizability in practice, given the scarcity of rigged samples due to the high cost of manual rigging.

controls.description: On meshes with multiple disconnected components (eyeballs, teeth, mouth socket), measure interpenetration between the inner components and the outer face surface after deformation (e.g. percentage of penetrating vertices), in addition to vertex error.
controls.evidence: We evaluate penetration between inner components (e.g., teeth) and the outer face surface by reporting the percentage of penetrating vertices

fruitful_directions.description: Scale training beyond the scarce rigged meshes by supervising unrigged neutral meshes in 2D: render each neutral mesh, synthesize posed images with a pretrained 2D face animation model (fine-tuned on renderings of rigged heads) driven by renderings of a rigged head's FACS poses, estimate 2D displacements with an optical flow model, and supervise the 3D deformation network through differentiable rendering; pretrain on all heads with 2D losses, then fine-tune on rigged heads with 3D and 2D losses.
fruitful_directions.evidence: Supported by a generative 2D face animation model that synthesizes posed images from the renderings of a neutral mesh, along with an optical flow estimator that predicts the 2D displacement between neutral and posed images as 2D supervisions, we expand the training dataset using unlabeled neutral meshes without rigs.

fruitful_directions.description: Supervise subtle expressions with a motion signal rather than appearance alone: a per-pixel 2D displacement field (optical-flow-like) rendered differentiably from the predicted 3D displacements and compared with a target displacement field, which stays informative where RGB changes are negligible (uniform regions such as cheeks, small poses such as jaw-left).
fruitful_directions.evidence: the 2D displacement is more distinguishable for subtle facial expressions because it explicitly represents the motion of each pixel in 2D, rather than relying on RGB value changes.

fruitful_directions.description: Use a triangulation-agnostic intrinsic surface network conditioned on the FACS pose vector, augmented with a mesh-level global feature (pooled over the vertices of all components and injected into every block) so that disconnected components such as eyeballs and teeth share information, deform coherently and avoid interpenetration.
fruitful_directions.evidence: These results demonstrate that the global feature effectively encodes both the position and presence of disconnected components, avoiding penetration and achieving accurate deformation.

sterile_directions.description: Supervising the 3D deformation in 2D with appearance-only losses (rendered RGB image and mask photometric losses) as the sole training signal for unrigged meshes: for subtle FACS poses the pixel differences are tiny, so the loss stays near its minimum even when the mesh is left undeformed.
sterile_directions.evidence: In other words, the magnitude of the loss remains minimal---even if the deformation model leaves all vertices fixed in the neutral expression.

sterile_directions.description: Applying a standard intrinsic surface network whose information propagates only along the surface (e.g. plain DiffusionNet), without any cross-component mechanism, to meshes with disconnected parts: information cannot flow between components, so they deform incoherently and interpenetrate.
sterile_directions.evidence: However, DiffusionNet struggles to handle multiple disconnected components as its diffusion mechanism cannot propagate information between them.

sterile_directions.description: Training the rigging network only on the small set of artist-rigged meshes with 3D supervision as the main strategy: the limited size and diversity of rigged data constrains generalization to unseen facial shapes and styles.
sterile_directions.evidence: Due to the high cost of manual rigging, this subset is limited in size, constraining the generalization ability of models trained exclusively on it.

taches.questions:
Facial rigging aims to make a static neutral facial mesh animatable by defining a set of controllable deformations, typically represented either as blendshape rigs driven by activated action units in systems based on the Facial Action Coding System (FACS), or as skeletal rigs driven by joint positions. Whereas full-body auto-rigging usually follows a two-step pipeline of skeleton construction and skinning, facial rigs are often anatomically inspired and implemented with FACS blendshapes. In a linear FACS blendshape rig, each blendshape is a vertex offset from the neutral mesh corresponding to one action unit, i.e. a specific muscle movement such as "Right Eye Close", and a complex expression is obtained by adding the weighted offsets of the activated blendshapes to the neutral mesh. Rigging is an essential step for creative AI, bringing digital avatars to life by enabling expressive and realistic facial movements across a wide range of applications. However, creating a facial rig is laborious and expensive, often requiring skilled artists tens of hours to complete a single asset. Methods that transfer expressions from 2D images or videos to 3D avatars do not remove this bottleneck, since they assume that the avatar already has a rig.

Existing facial auto-rigging methods typically transfer a complete set of blendshapes from a predefined template mesh to a neutral target mesh, which often requires dense correspondences or a mesh topology shared by the template and the target. More recent approaches build transferable latent spaces between faces or use triangulation-agnostic networks to bypass these limitations, but they still require a template blendshape rig, which can compromise accuracy when the template and target shapes differ substantially. Only one prior approach, NFR, can directly rig facial meshes from explicitly controllable FACS parameters without relying on a template, and it has so far been demonstrated primarily on humanoid heads. Furthermore, existing approaches, NFR included, have yet to accommodate meshes with multiple disconnected components, such as eyeballs or teeth, which limits their ability to animate highly expressive avatars: an "eye look-down" pose, for example, is difficult to reproduce if the mesh lacks eyeballs.

Learning such a rigging model also raises a data problem. Accurate 3D supervision requires neutral meshes paired with complete rigs made by artists, and because manual rigging is so costly such rigged examples are scarce; a model trained solely on them is likely to generalize poorly to the wide variety of facial shapes, styles and topologies met in practice.

The problem is therefore to automatically turn a single static neutral facial mesh into an expressive rig controllable by FACS parameters (i) without relying on predefined template blendshapes, so that target meshes need not closely resemble a template; (ii) for in-the-wild meshes with varying topologies and shapes, including both humanoid and non-humanoid heads; and (iii) for meshes made of multiple disconnected components, such as eyeballs and teeth, which must move coherently with the rest of the face. How can such a rigging system be built, and how can it be trained to generalize across this diversity when only a limited number of rigged meshes is available as 3D ground truth?

compute.evidence: Not reported in GPU-hours: the paper only states that all experiments ran on an NVIDIA TITAN GPU and gives average training time per iteration (late fusion / late fusion + MNL: 21/31 ms on MVSA, 69/86 ms on Food-101, 32/49 ms on NYU Depth V2, 63/87 ms on CREMA-D). Estimate: cost is dominated by UPMC Food-101 (about 100,000 image-text pairs; assume about 60,000 for training): about 3,750 iterations per epoch at batch size 16 x 100 epochs x about 0.086 s = about 9 GPU-hours per run; 3 MNL-integrated variants (late fusion, QMF, PDF) x 5 seeds = 15 runs = about 135 GPU-hours. MVSA, NYU Depth V2 and CREMA-D runs (assumed about 1.5k, 0.8k and 6.7k training samples, 100 epochs, batch 16/32/64) take minutes each, so their 5-seed main runs, the CREMA-D baselines reproduced by the authors, the guidance ablations, the lambda and warm-up sweeps, the 200-epoch runs, the latent-fusion comparisons and CMU-MOSEI add about 30-50 GPU-hours; LoRA fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-1.5B on MathQA and of Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct on 6,993 Visual7W examples adds about 10-20 GPU-hours. That is about 190 GPU-hours of pure iteration time; with about 1.5x for data loading and evaluation under several noise settings, about 300 GPU-hours. The total could be several times higher if models were retrained for each noise setting or if the Food-101 competing methods were rerun rather than reported from prior implementations.

controls.description: Unimodal baselines: each modality's model trained and evaluated alone (e.g., image-only, text-only, audio-only, visual-only) with the same backbones, training and noise conditions, to quantify the imbalance between modalities and to check whether the weak modality itself benefits.
controls.evidence: In addition, we establish unimodal baselines to provide a comprehensive evaluation.

controls.description: Standard late fusion baselines on the same backbones and training configuration: plain static late fusion (equal-weight logit fusion trained with cross-entropy only) and state-of-the-art dynamic or uncertainty-aware late fusion methods (e.g., DynMM, TMC, QMF, PDF); the proposed training scheme is compared against them and, if it is an add-on, applied on top of both static and dynamic fusion.
controls.evidence: Specifically, we compare our method against representative static fusion strategies as well as state-of-the-art dynamic fusion techniques such as DynMM [@xue2023dynamic], TMC [@han2022trusted], QMF [@zhang2023provable], and PDF [@cao2024predictive].

controls.description: An alignment-based guidance baseline: the weak modality is pushed to imitate the dominant modality's prediction over the whole label space (e.g., KL-divergence or knowledge-distillation alignment), compared head-to-head with the proposed way of helping the weak modality under the same fusion model.
controls.evidence: All-Class guidance, which aligns inferior modalities across the full label space

controls.description: Robustness evaluation under controlled, modality-appropriate input corruption at several graded severity levels including the clean setting (e.g., Gaussian and salt noise on images, reduced signal-to-noise ratio on audio, blanked or masked text, applied to part of the modalities), not only clean accuracy.
controls.evidence: we evaluate average model performance under Gaussian and Salt noise for image modality, SNR-based noise for audio modality, and blank noise for the text modality.

controls.description: Several independent random seeds (e.g., five) per configuration, with mean and standard deviation reported, so that small gains can be distinguished from run-to-run variance.
controls.evidence: To reduce the variance introduced by stochastic factors, we conduct evaluations using five independent random seeds.

controls.description: Diagnostics of the weak modality beyond fused accuracy: its own branch accuracy with versus without the proposed training, and a quantitative measure of the modality-specific information it retains (e.g., unique information via partial information decomposition, or divergence between modality predictions), to check that it is not simply over-aligned with the dominant modality.

taches.questions:
Multimodal learning has become a cornerstone of many real-world applications, such as autonomous perception, medical diagnosis, and human-computer interaction. By integrating information from multiple sources, such as vision, audio, and text, multimodal systems aim to improve performance and generalization. However, multimodal data often exhibit a significant imbalance between modalities due to noise, lack of information, or sensor heterogeneity, so that a dominant modality may overshadow the others and hinder the learning of weak modalities. Unimodal prediction accuracy is widely used to detect modality imbalance; it is a simple and effective metric, but it is inherently sensitive to noise and perturbations. This vulnerability often leads to fragile performance in practice and limits the reliability of accuracy-based definitions of strong and weak modalities in real-world deployments.

Modality imbalance arises in early, intermediate, and late fusion alike. Late fusion, also known as decision-level fusion, combines the outputs (logits) of modality-specific models, either with equal weights (static late fusion) or with weights that vary across samples (dynamic late fusion). It remains one of the most widely adopted paradigms because of its modular design, interpretability, and strong compatibility with unimodal pre-trained models. Yet, lacking feature-level compensation or cross-modal interaction, late fusion tends to amplify the influence of strong modalities while weakening the role of lower-quality ones, so that predictions from disadvantaged modalities often carry little weight or even introduce noise into the final decision. A large body of work has attempted to alleviate this imbalance by enhancing the predictive performance of weak modalities, for example by aggregating independently trained modality-specific classifiers, confidence-based weighting, modality dropout or gating, adaptive ensembling, or knowledge distillation from dominant modalities.

While effective in certain scenarios, these methods often implicitly aim to align weak modalities with dominant ones in terms of prediction accuracy, attempting to bring them closer to their stronger counterparts. Such over-alignment raises several concerns: (1) it may suppress the distinct and complementary information encoded in weak modalities, causing modality-specific information loss; (2) it risks error propagation, as the dominant modality's errors are amplified when weak modalities follow them blindly; and (3) through excessive conformity, weak modalities may lose the predictive advantages they originally held on some samples.

Robustness makes the issue more pressing. Multimodal cooperation is inherently sensitive to perturbations such as data noise, label noise, and incomplete modalities, because modalities are heterogeneous and vary in reliability in real-world conditions. Prior studies have highlighted that the robustness of a multimodal system can be bottlenecked by a single weak modality, revealing a strong link between modality imbalance and overall system reliability. Existing work addresses robustness by incorporating uncertainty modeling, designing robustness-aware fusion strategies, quantifying multimodal robustness with dedicated evaluation metrics, or connecting it with generalization error bounds. However, most of these approaches emphasize prediction-consistency modeling and pay little attention to the instability of the decision space, that is, a model's high sensitivity to input perturbations near the decision boundary, where even minor changes can cause large shifts in prediction; they also tend to require more complex architectures with limited generalizability across tasks with different class granularity.

This raises several questions. How can a dominant modality help a weak modality within a decision-level fusion system without forcing it to conform, so that the weak modality keeps its unique, complementary information and does not inherit the dominant modality's errors? Given that judging modality strength by unimodal accuracy or confidence is itself fragile under noise, how can one reliably determine which modality is dominant and which is weak? How do the predictions of the individual modalities determine the robustness of the fused decision to input perturbations, and can a remedy for modality imbalance come with a theoretical guarantee on that robustness? Finally, can such a remedy both narrow the performance gap between modalities and make the fused prediction more reliable under noisy and imbalanced conditions?

taches.questions:
Transformers, powered by attention mechanisms, have become the default backbone for sequence modeling across language, vision, speech, and decision making. Their success is often linked to selective access to an ever-growing key-value cache while retaining parallel training and inference. In large language models, this selective ability, composed across multiple attention layers and residual pathways, supports long-range memory retrieval and the algorithmic behaviors associated with in-context learning (for example induction heads and pattern completion), as shown by empirical and mechanistic studies.

Causal softmax attention combines strong selectivity with parallel efficiency: at each step it forms a distribution over past indices and mixes their values, while all steps can be computed in parallel. Given queries, keys and values $Q,K,V\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d}$ with rows $q_t$, $k_i$, $v_i$, define masked scores $s_{t,i}=q_t^\top k_i/\sqrt{d}$ for $i\le t$ and $-\infty$ otherwise, and set $\alpha_{t,\cdot}=\mathrm{softmax}(s_{t,\cdot})$, a probability distribution over $\{1,\dots,t\}$. The step-$t$ read is $o_t=\sum_{i\le t}\alpha_{t,i}v_i$, which lies in the convex hull of $\{v_1,\dots,v_t\}$; stacking all steps yields $O=AV$ with $A_{t,i}=\alpha_{t,i}$, so a single matrix multiply produces all outputs.

This convex-mixture view explains the efficiency of attention, but it also reveals a dilemma between lossless storage and lossy processing. The key-value cache stores the full context, but the read is lossy: each head applies the same weights to all coordinates of $v_i$, so the output lies in the convex hull of the stored values and all channels are synchronized. As a result, even simple per-channel indexing, such as returning $(v_{i_1,1},\dots,v_{i_D,D})$ where each coordinate $j$ is taken from its own past index $i_j$ (for example, a coordinate-wise argmax), cannot be represented unless all chosen indices coincide. This limitation hinders Transformers in long-range modeling with non-sequential or irregular timestep indexing, and in tasks where channel-wise structure is critical, such as multivariate time series modeling.

Most recent advances in attention aim to improve expressivity and efficiency, typically by designing richer selection distributions while still reading values through a token-separable linear combination. These include sparse attention patterns, low-rank projections, and kernelizable variants with normalization or gating. Efficiency-oriented work accelerates attention through factorized implementations, or replaces the cache with streaming state space models and recurrent networks that keep a fixed-size state. Across these lines, computation becomes faster or the distribution richer, but the read remains a linear mix: channels share weights, and even simple per-channel indexing cannot be realized in one step. Some recent works explore more complex combinations, such as nonlinear mixing or hard/top-k selection, yet these mainly target training stability or accuracy in specific cases and do not address the lossy-processing limitation.

This leaves an open problem: how can the read of an attention-style sequence mixer be redesigned to remove this linear read bottleneck and support per-channel, context-dependent selection from memory, so that different channels can retrieve different past indices in the same step, while keeping causal parallelism and the asymptotic time complexity of the underlying selection mechanism (for example, quadratic in sequence length for softmax attention and linear for linear-time variants)? And does closing this gap between lossless storage and lossy processing translate into better sequence modeling in practice?

taches.questions:
In cloud services, Internet of Things deployments and monitoring systems, data are often represented as univariate time series (UTS), in which each timestamp records a single variable. Anomalies arise, for instance, when a website is subject to malicious attacks or experiences excessive server load, and they are typically reflected in UTS derived from traffic and system-load monitoring. Missed or delayed detection of such events can have severe consequences. Anomalies in UTS are usually divided into two types: point anomalies, which are abrupt deviations (either global or contextual), and segment anomalies, which reflect more subtle shifts in trends or periodic patterns.

Formally, given observations x_0, x_1, ..., x_t with anomaly labels c_0, c_1, ..., c_t, where c_i = 0 marks a normal point and c_i = 1 an anomaly, the goal of UTS anomaly detection is to determine c_i for each point x_i from the history x_0, ..., x_{i-1} that precedes it, without access to future points. Because labels are scarce in practice and supervised detectors generalize poorly under label scarcity or distribution shift, unsupervised approaches have become the dominant paradigm. Reconstruction-based and prediction-based methods both model normal behavior and flag anomalies by comparing reconstructed or predicted values with the actual observations. Reconstruction-based techniques try to map abnormal segments to a normal space, but the lack of ground truth for anomalies leads to poor reconstruction and degraded performance, and they treat time windows independently, ignoring temporal dependencies. Prediction-based methods built on deep sequence models such as Transformers perform strongly on multivariate time series, where they can model complex dependencies; in UTS, however, each timestamp contains only one value, which restricts the representation of temporal context and leads to suboptimal performance.

In particular, existing detectors struggle with two kinds of subtle anomalies that remain largely undetected: (1) small point anomalies, short-term spikes that look normal when viewed over longer windows; and (2) slowly rising anomalies, gradual segment-level deviations from periodic patterns. These misses stem from limitations of current designs: for example, a frequency-conditioned reconstruction approach focuses on frequency components rather than local dependencies and fails to capture subtle point anomalies or gradual segment anomalies, while a recent prediction approach uses timing information but ignores frequency details.

Detecting these anomalies raises three challenges. First, local trends matter more than absolute values: the absolute magnitude of a change is insufficient to decide whether a point is anomalous. In one series, changes between 0.5 and 1 may be abnormal, whereas in another, similar changes are normal and only variations exceeding 5 are anomalous; what counts as abnormal depends on the value distribution and change patterns within a short local window. Second, periodicity evolves rather than staying static: time series exhibit evolving trends and periodicity, and periodicity varies over time and across datasets, including changes in period length and frequency. Without future points, distinguishing slow anomalies from normal periodic changes is difficult, and methods that focus only on the adjacent historical period neglect this evolution; modeling periodicity that is both dynamic and heterogeneous is hard. Third, normal patterns must be learned amid anomalies and noise: real-world series contain long-term noise and sudden anomalies, both of which hinder the learning of normal patterns. Noise introduces significant fluctuations that make it difficult to fit the underlying normal behavior, and the lack of ground-truth labels for anomaly positions prevents a model from computing reliable training losses.

The question is therefore how an unsupervised detector for univariate time series, relying only on past observations, can capture both local trends and the evolution of periodic patterns, while learning normal behavior robustly from training data contaminated by noise and unlabeled anomalies, so that small point anomalies and slowly rising anomalies are detected accurately and promptly.

taches.questions:
Large language models have recently improved their reasoning by spending more test-time compute, generating more tokens before producing a final answer. Extended sequential scaling has limits, however: beyond a certain length, performance can decrease because of "overthinking", and long sequential reasoning can be sensitive to the order of reasoning steps. A complementary scaling dimension, repeated parallel sampling followed by aggregation, as in self-consistency (majority voting) or Best-of-N selection, has further boosted reasoning performance. These parallel methods rely on the model generating solutions that are both diverse and correct, and as tasks become harder, some mechanism for increasing diversity becomes necessary.

Obtaining such diversity is difficult. Only a minority of tokens in a chain of thought act as forking tokens that lead to distinct reasoning modes, so as problems become harder and generations longer, these tokens become substantially harder to sample. The common practice for encouraging diversity, raising the sampling temperature, inherently entails a diversity-accuracy trade-off, because the forking tokens that trigger diverse yet correct reasoning modes typically lie deep within the sampling tree. Theoretical work further shows that increasing the temperature alone does not necessarily yield greater diversity unless the model has been explicitly trained to ensure coverage. Search-based alternatives such as Monte Carlo tree search or Tree of Thoughts increase coverage through heuristic-guided search with an external verifier, but their reliance on heuristics and domain-specific knowledge limits the tasks to which they apply. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards is not a complete answer either: it requires a strong base model, and recent work suggests that it does not by itself instill new capabilities, so what a model learns during fine-tuning matters.

At the same time, several distinct and correct reasoning traces per question can be obtained at low cost and without human annotation, for instance by distilling from different teacher models, sampling repeatedly, and filtering with a verifiable correctness check. This suggests training models for coverage directly from such diverse traces, but how to do so is unclear. Standard supervised fine-tuning treats each trace as an independent example and has no explicit mechanism for keeping different reasoning modes apart: it is an open question whether the modes are preserved or merged into one, and whether a particular mode can later be deliberately elicited. Recent efforts to train models natively for parallel reasoning, by converting sequential chains of thought into parallel ones or by training on multiple traces distilled from teachers, show that native parallel scaling can surpass sequential scaling within certain token limits, but they leave open whether the distinct reasoning modes present in the training traces are actually retained and can be reliably triggered.

The problem is therefore how to fine-tune a language model on a set of diverse, correct reasoning traces per question so that it retains their distinct reasoning modes rather than collapsing them, and so that diverse yet accurate reasoning paths can be reliably triggered when sampling in parallel, instead of depending on sampling rare forking tokens deep inside a generation. Can such training improve both the accuracy of a single generation and the accuracy and coverage obtained by aggregating a small number of parallel generations?

taches.questions:
Knowledge distillation is a fundamental technique in machine learning, widely used for model compression, transfer learning, and improving generalization. Its core idea is to transfer knowledge from a "teacher" model to a (typically smaller) "student" model by training the student to match the teacher's output probabilities rather than categorical one-hot labels. This softened supervision has been shown to improve performance across a range of tasks. Consequently, a substantial body of research has focused on designing distillation mechanisms, such as dynamic temperature scaling, feature-based distillation, and task-aware teacher-student matching, typically assuming a large teacher that is optimized to maximize its own performance.

Despite its widespread adoption, the theoretical foundations of knowledge distillation remain only partially understood. In particular, the impact of the teacher's output probabilities on the student's optimization trajectory and generalization has not been fully characterized. Existing explanations attribute the usefulness of distillation to the regularizing effect of the teacher's soft estimates, to trade-offs such as precision versus recall or knowledge inheritance versus exploration, or to factors such as data geometry and optimization bias. Insights into how distillation affects the optimization itself have been developed only for special cases, such as self-distillation or a student that is a compressed version of the teacher, and rely on dedicated gradient approximations. A principled understanding of how distillation affects common learning algorithms, such as stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and its variants, for arbitrary teachers, is still lacking.

Recent works have begun to view distillation through a Bayesian lens, interpreting the teacher's outputs as (possibly noisy) estimates of the true class posterior probabilities of the data-generating distribution. From this statistical viewpoint, learning from accurate class posteriors has been argued to reduce the variance of the student's objective, and excess-risk and generalization bounds have been derived in terms of the distance between the teacher's predictions and the true posteriors. These analyses, however, characterize the statistical properties of the risk rather than the behavior of the learning algorithm that actually trains the student. The probabilistic perspective thus opens relatively unexplored questions about the dynamics of SGD-based learning under probabilistic supervision, and about how the statistical calibration of the teacher influences the student. Teacher calibration has been recognized as a key driver of distillation, but it remains unclear how the quality of the teacher's probability estimates should guide the way teachers are built.

This raises several questions. How does supervising a student with the exact class posterior probabilities, instead of one-hot labels, change the convergence behavior and stability of SGD-based learning and the generalization of the resulting student? In the realistic case where the teacher provides only imperfect, noisy estimates of these posteriors, how does the level of estimation error affect the student's convergence, generalization and accuracy, and under what conditions does probabilistic supervision remain preferable to one-hot labels? Finally, what practical guidelines follow for designing or choosing teacher models, beyond maximizing the teacher's own accuracy, so that their outputs provide better supervision for students trained with SGD-based optimizers?

taches.questions:
Large language models (LLMs) have made remarkable progress across a wide range of natural language understanding and generation tasks, but their massive parameter counts demand prohibitively large computational and memory resources for both training and deployment. Even in settings with a reasonable amount of compute, training or fine-tuning such models remains challenging.

One promising way to reduce the computational burden of fine-tuning is low-precision floating-point (FP) arithmetic such as FP8. Modern accelerators (e.g., NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell GPUs, AMD CDNA 3, Google TPUs) increasingly support low-precision FP arithmetic natively, and FP8 can theoretically double the throughput of FP16 matrix multiplication. Because FP8 formats (such as E4M3 or E5M2) have a narrow representable range, a higher-precision tensor must first be scaled by a per-tensor factor obtained from a max-reduction over its absolute values, and then scaled element-wise and rounded, before the low-precision multiplication can run. This quantization overhead is memory-bound and grows quadratically with matrix size, whereas the cost of matrix multiplication grows cubically. As a consequence, FP8 is known to accelerate mainly large-dimensional matrix multiplications (empirically, when each matrix dimension exceeds roughly 4K elements), while small-dimensional computations can even suffer an unexpected slowdown.

These overheads are especially critical for low-rank adaptation (LoRA), a widely used approach to parameter-efficient fine-tuning. LoRA keeps the pretrained weights frozen and inserts small trainable low-rank matrices (adapters) that capture task-specific knowledge, greatly reducing memory cost by training few parameters. For such small-dimensional matrices, the overhead of FP8 quantization can outweigh the gains of FP8 multiplication, and the separate forward and backward paths of the adapters add further quantization operations at every iteration. Yet fast LoRA fine-tuning matters in practice: many applications require training numerous adapters, for example one adapter per user for personalized recommendation or personalized alignment from human feedback, task-specific adapters for multi-task learning and mixtures of LoRA experts, adapters for different domains, multilingual summarization, and rapid updates in dynamic, user-specific environments. Efficiently accelerating LoRA fine-tuning is therefore essential for timely, scalable and cost-effective adaptation of LLMs under practical computational constraints.

Existing lines of work leave this gap open. Quantized LoRA methods (such as QLoRA with 4-bit NormalFloat weights, QA-LoRA with group-wise INT4 weights, and follow-ups that refine the quantization with integer linear programming, SVD-based adapter initialization, dynamic rank allocation or information recovery) compress the frozen backbone through weight-only quantization. They focus on memory efficiency rather than fine-tuning speed: the added quantization and dequantization often make them slower than standard LoRA, and weight-only quantization cannot exploit hardware acceleration of low-precision matrix multiplication. Conversely, FP8 training methods (hybrid E4M3/E5M2 formats, mixed-precision FP8 training with high-precision master weights, studies of large-scale FP8 stability and outliers, unit scaling) are designed for the large-dimensional matrices of full LLM training, not for the small matrices that characterize LoRA.

This raises the following questions. How large is the quantization overhead when FP8 arithmetic is applied to LoRA fine-tuning, which parts of the computation does it come from, and does it persist across typical adapter ranks? Can LoRA fine-tuning be organized so that it genuinely benefits from native FP8 arithmetic, delivering real end-to-end speedups over existing quantized LoRA methods, while retaining the memory savings that make LoRA attractive and reaching accuracy comparable to existing quantized LoRA fine-tuning?

taches.questions:
Traditional multimodal models are typically divided into two categories: multimodal understanding (e.g., answering questions about images) and multimodal generation (e.g., generating images from text prompts). Unified Multimodal Generative Models (UMGMs) aim to integrate these two capabilities within a single framework. Recent UMGMs have demonstrated strong performance on a wide range of tasks, such as visual question answering, image captioning, visual reasoning, classification, reading comprehension, and image generation. They typically embed multiple input types into a shared representation space and use one single autoregressive transformer backbone to model cross-modal interactions, so that the same model produces both textual and visual outputs. Training generally follows a two-stage paradigm: pretraining focused on text-image alignment, followed by fine-tuning for specific downstream tasks, where instruction tuning (fine-tuning on diverse, task-specific instructions paired with expected outputs) has become a widely adopted strategy for aligning model behavior with human intent.

Although UMGMs show impressive zero-shot performance on many unseen instructions, their effectiveness is inconsistent across tasks, particularly when the relevant task data is absent from the pretraining corpus. Adding new task data to the training set can substantially improve performance on those tasks, but because novel multimodal tasks keep emerging, repeatedly merging new data and retraining the model is computationally expensive and impractical. This calls for ways to let UMGMs adapt flexibly and efficiently over time, in line with the principles of continual learning, where models acquire new capabilities incrementally.

Studies in continual learning have shown that sequentially fine-tuned models suffer from catastrophic forgetting: a model fine-tuned on new tasks tends to forget or overwrite previously acquired knowledge. Several works have explored continual instruction tuning for multimodal large language models, with methods that are typically regularization-based, architecture-based, replay-based, or prompt-based, and mixture-of-experts adapters have also attracted growing attention in continual learning for their scalability and modularity. However, these multimodal models produce language-only outputs, so prior research has focused exclusively on multimodal understanding tasks such as visual question answering, and existing methods address only intra-modal catastrophic forgetting, where old tasks, new tasks, and pre-trained capabilities all belong to the same output modality, typically text. This assumption holds for multimodal models with unimodal outputs, but it is insufficient for UMGMs, which generate both text and images from a single backbone. For UMGMs, forgetting may occur not only within a modality (intra-modal) but also across modalities (inter-modal): for example, continually tuning the model on a sequence of multimodal understanding tasks might erode its pre-trained image generation ability. This inter-modal forgetting remains largely unexplored, and it is unclear whether methods designed for the intra-modal setting can handle both forms of forgetting at once.

The central question is therefore: can UMGMs continually acquire new capabilities through instruction tuning without suffering catastrophic forgetting, both within a modality (e.g., multimodal understanding) and across modalities (e.g., improving multimodal understanding while preserving visual generation)? Answering it requires establishing whether inter-modal forgetting actually occurs in UMGMs, explaining what causes it, and finding an efficient way to adapt these models to new tasks that retains performance on earlier tasks as well as the pre-trained capabilities of the other modality.

fruitful_directions.description: Hybrid explicit-implicit representation: keep a sparse set of compact explicit Gaussians that store only a few high-frequency-critical attributes (position, isotropic scale, opacity, diffuse color) and let grid-based neural fields predict the remaining properties (anisotropic shape, rotation, view-dependent color), adding the neural predictions to the explicit values as residuals.
fruitful_directions.evidence: Our key insight is to decompose the representation into two complementary components: grid-based neural fields that capture low-frequency variations, and a sparse set of explicit compact Gaussians that preserve high-frequency details.

fruitful_directions.description: Decouple geometry and appearance into two separate neural fields, one predicting scale, opacity and rotation and one predicting view-dependent color from position and view direction, instead of a single shared field.
fruitful_directions.evidence: the single neural field exhibits consistent degradation across all image quality metrics

fruitful_directions.description: Hybrid rendering: cull Gaussians outside the view frustum before querying the neural fields to keep real-time speed, and model distant content with a neural-field-predicted background (colors on a large background sphere) alpha-composited with the transmittance left after the Gaussian foreground.
fruitful_directions.evidence: disabling background rendering results in significantly degraded visual quality, despite offering only marginal improvements in rendering speed

sterile_directions.description: Compressing 3DGS by naively encoding all Gaussian properties in a fixed-resolution grid-based neural field, with no explicit per-Gaussian attributes: it misses high-frequency content and fails on thin structures and high-frequency colors.
sterile_directions.evidence: As a result, naively fitting 3D Gaussians to neural fields often fails to reconstruct fine details, such as thin geometric structures and high-frequency color variations.
sterile_directions.section: Introduction (supported by the Explicit Gaussians ablation in Model Analysis)

sterile_directions.description: Predicting all Gaussian properties, geometry and view-dependent color together, from a single shared neural field.
sterile_directions.evidence: Empirical results demonstrate that predicting all Gaussian properties through a single neural field fails to achieve satisfactory performance.
sterile_directions.section: Methodology - Hybrid Radiance Fields (Decoupled neural fields)

sterile_directions.description: Saving memory simply by reducing Gaussians to isotropic shapes with diffuse (view-independent) color, without any neural or other model of anisotropy and view-dependent effects.
sterile_directions.evidence: Without these neural components, our framework falls back to isotropic Gaussians with diffuse shading which has limited representation capacity, leading to a noticeable degradation in novel view synthesis quality
